#214. Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable

An independent browser engine arrives on Linux and macOS, and we’ve tried it.

Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault.

After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it’s an installable package with automatic updating.

Ladybird is most notable for what it isn’t: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google’s Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird’s rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. “The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork,” project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday’s announcement. “The browser around it is modest, but functional.”

Nearly the entire modern web currently runs on three browser engines. There’s WebKit (Safari), Gecko (Firefox), and the biggest of them all, Blink (Chromium). Those limited options mean that web developers often end up optimizing sites for Chromium specifically, since that’s where the majority of traffic is, and as a result, the whole web platform tends to follow suit toward whatever the dominant engine supports.

An independent implementation of web standards has value not just by providing additional competition in the market, but because it can’t help but reveal places where sites depend on Chromium behaviors rather than published specifications. The fact that Ladybird exists isn’t likely to shift the market tides any time soon, but every new browser engine increases the number of implementations that standards can be tested against, which can surface Chromium-specific assumptions and push the ecosystem toward the spec.

The Ladybird project was borne out of Kling’s SerenityOS project, an attempt to develop a new independent OS from scratch, before splitting off as a separate project. Kling formed the Ladybird Browser Initiative, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by sponsorships and donations. The project’s site highlights that there are no sponsored search engine deals supporting the project like many other popular browsers, and sponsoring entities have no say in the project roadmap.

The Ladybird alpha is a rolling release channel that updates automatically, and the downloadable package is a huge step to getting the browser onto the PCs of everyday users. “Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that,” Kling wrote. Though the browser began as C++, in keeping with the ethos of SerenityOS, the project has since started shifting toward Rust, starting with its JavaScript engine.

While it’s exciting to have a new engine option for browsing, the project leader notes that this is still a very early release. The browser build contains a built-in tool for reporting any websites that fail to render or crash the browser. Kling writes, “We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today.”

Microsoft users are still out in the cold on this one for now. The project says that future support for Windows is planned, but it’s macOS and Linux only for now.

I tested the Ladybird alpha version 2026.47.8 on my AceMagic W1 mini PC AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS with 16GB DDR5 and running Fedora Linux 44 with the new KDE Plasma 6.8.3, and the most surprising thing about the alpha build was how little it feels like alpha software.

The browser seemed to handle most anything I threw at it without issue. Day-to-day tabbed browsing mechanics felt snappy and normal. A 50MB test video file downloaded quickly and smoothly. With a dozen tabs open, switching between them was instant, and the browser felt responsive throughout. Options menus were surprisingly fleshed out for a build this young.

Google Maps loaded instantly, located me, and handled everything I threw at it: adding and removing layers, zooming out from the Midwest, and dropping into Street View in Alberta, Canada in around three seconds. Everything rendered fast enough that my mini PC’s fan spun up noticeably. GitHub’s site, including repository navigation, worked without a hitch. So did YouTube and the news sites I tried.

I could stall the browser, but it took some effort. With about 10 tabs open, I was streaming a 4K test video file from my personal Jellyfin server. Everything worked fine at first, but after skipping around in the file over and over again, the browser eventually got stuck. Mind you, this is an alpha build that I was trying to trip up, not a representation of something inherently broken.

After spending an evening with Ladybird, I can say that while it won’t be replacing Firefox for me anytime soon, I was genuinely impressed that a scratch-made engine could perform this well in such an early state. Most new browser projects are forks of something that already exists. Ladybird is the rare exception, an engine written from nothing, and the alpha runs well enough that if you have a Mac or Linux PC handy, it’s worth downloading a build and poking around yourself. Just remember Kling’s warning: This is nowhere near trustworthy enough to make your daily driver, yet.

What the alpha demonstrates is that a small team of independent developers, funded by donations, has built a browser engine from scratch that handles real web browsing without a fuss. That it works this well this soon, using no existing engine code, is an achievement. I thought I was a Firefox loyalist, but I’ll be keeping an eye on where this one goes.

#213. Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a new battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their new mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s plans planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he said.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had said the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government plans. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu said he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he said.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.

#212. What to do if your Apple apps start showing subscription retention messages

Some apps can now show you a message, or even a discount, when you try to cancel a subscription.

Canceling a subscription on your iPhone or iPad is usually quick. All you need to do is go to the Subscriptions menu in Settings. However, some apps may be a little more persistent before letting you cancel because of a recent Apple update for developers.

Earlier this month, Apple introduced subscription retention messages, which give developers a way to convince you to stay, whether with a message or even a special discount. So if an app keeps urging you to stay, it isn't breaking any App Store rules, and there's nothing to worry about. Here's how Apple's subscription retention messages work and what they mean for you.

For example, an app might offer you a free trial or a discount on your next monthly payment if you're eligible and decide to stay. It's up to you whether to keep your subscription, and you'll see Cancel Subscription and Keep Subscription buttons. If an offer is available, there will be a Redeem button too. Developers have to set these features up, so not every app will show you a retention message or offer. Developers can create these messages through App Store Connect, the platform they also use to distribute apps to Apple devices.

Messages and offers may also vary between users of the same app, since developers can set up a specific offer for people who have paid for a minimum subscription period. Each app can have up to 10 different retention messages. Developers who want more control can request access to the Apple Retention Messaging API, which requires review and approval by Apple. The retention messages can also highlight what you'll miss out on if you cancel a subscription, such as access to exclusive in-app content.

That doesn't mean you get nothing out of this feature. If you were planning to cancel a subscription because it's too expensive, a retention offer can give you the same service for less, at least for a while. It's worth reading the message before confirming to see how long the discount will last and what the price will be once the offer ends. And if you really want to cancel, nothing changes for you. Just tap Cancel Subscription and you won't be asked about it again.

Unfortunately, there's no way to turn off these retention messages, but they only appear when you try to cancel a subscription. They won't pop up out of nowhere while you're using your iPhone or iPad. Keep in mind that these retention messages require iOS 15.1 or later. They're also available on the latest versions of macOS and visionOS. It might also be a good time to find and cancel subscriptions you're not using.

I have to be honest here: most streaming deals aren't going to turn your finances around in any life-changing way. The Black Friday streaming price cuts have become steadily less tempting over the past few years. They're just not as impressive as they used to be. It's also worth noting that most deals apply only to the ad-supported tiers (with just a few exceptions). Still, any and every discount is welcome in a time when prices keep rising. Every cent counts, and it's easy to lose track of just how much you spend on streaming — especially if you're signed up for more than one service.

Most streamers announced their Black Friday deals ahead of the big day, but you may be wondering if there are still more to come. With just a couple of days until Cyber Monday, I'd say the best streaming deals have already arrived. I can't imagine that many more will pop up at this stage.

I'm shocked that Peacock's Black Friday deal is as good as it is for 2026. Last year, the streamer didn't offer a deal at all, so this is light-years better than I was expecting. If you've been holding off on subscribing, now is likely the only time you'll get a decent discount. The Paramount+, HBO Max, and Disney+/Hulu Black Friday offers are pretty much on par with their deals of years past. I would lock in HBO Max and the Disney+/Hulu bundle for a full year, as more price increases could pop up in 2027. Paramount+ tends to offer discounts throughout the year more than any other streamer, so if you miss out on this one, it's no biggie.

It's not worth holding on for a Netflix Black Friday deal, unfortunately. Netflix has never offered a Black Friday discount, or any kind of discount for that matter. Netflix is the top name in streaming and apparently feels that it doesn't need to offer Black Friday deals. I don't expect this year to be any different, but I'm always willing to be proven wrong. It would be a nice and welcome surprise. If you do want to save a little money on a Netflix subscription, Costco is offering $100 gift cards for $89.99. It's not much, but like I said, every cent counts.

We'll be updating this list of the best Black Friday streaming deals on the off chance any more turn up, so be sure to check back for updates.

In case you missed it, the Thanksgiving Day parade was postponed for the first time in history due to weather. Instead of airing live on Thanksgiving Day as usual, it will air on Saturday, Nov. 28 at 8:30 a.m. You can stream the parade live on Peacock on Saturday or watch last year's parade on Thanksgiving Day. The Peacock Select tier will not grant you access; you'll need a Premium subscription.

Unfortunately, Netflix is one of the only streamers that just straight up does not participate in Black Friday. We've never seen a discounted subscription in years past and don't expect one in 2026. Costco is offering $100 Netflix gift cards for $89.99, so that might be your best bet to save on Netflix this year.

The majority of Black Friday streaming deals will carry over to Cyber Monday. But there likely won't be any new deals popping up specifically for Cyber Monday. Streamers that dropped Black Friday discounts this year will, for the most part, keep their offers live through the end of the day on Nov. 30.

#210. The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites

This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.

In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.

If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.

“The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.

This announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the company wide latitude as it works through these remaining issues.

For example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight.

The authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The company sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into “Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” That is, instead of burning them up in Earth’s atmosphere, SpaceX wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other orbits around Earth, or potentially into orbit around the Sun.

The FCC did not grant this waiver request “because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements.” The company will need to obtain a waiver before deploying any Starmind satellites that are not intended to be disposed of via atmospheric reentry.

However, in other ways the FCC appears to have been incredibly lenient with SpaceX. This is particularly the case with environmental concerns raised by numerous parties that commented on SpaceX’s application to the FCC.

Half a dozen organizations, such as the Secure World Foundation and American Astronomical Society, raised concerns about deploying so many satellites into orbit, citing collision risks, orbital debris, atmospheric pollution from so many satellite reentries, impacts on astronomical observations, and more. The FCC also received approximately 1,500 public comments concerning SpaceX’s application.

Some of these environmental issues, the FCC said, lay beyond the scope of its review. For example, on concerns about the environmental implications of thousands or potentially tens of thousands of rocket launches, the FCC said, “Potential concerns related to the emissions of rocket launches and the subsequent impacts on the human environment as an indirect result of the Starmind system are outside of the Commission’s purview.”

The FCC also rejected calls for further environmental scrutiny of pollution from satellite reentries, including concerns about aluminum oxides and their potential effects on the ozone layer. “Other concerns, including impacts on the atmosphere caused by satellites burning up on re-entry, remain speculative and not supported in the record,” the FCC authorization states.

As part of its decision, the FCC cited a significant policy change adopted in October, when the agency concluded that space-based activities generally fall outside its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC reasoned that as these activities occur beyond US territory, they don’t constitute federal actions requiring environmental review. As a result, the agency declined to conduct a comprehensive environmental assessment of SpaceX’s Starmind constellation.

With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#209. How you can give your old DJI drone new purpose

You don’t need to risk a brand new DJI drone for practice, specific tasks and aerial pics.

An old DJI drone is still a nice, working drone, and unless it's a wrecked heap of scrap, it has plenty of life ahead of it. Besides, it's a much better teacher than a new DJI Matrice 5T, because crashing it is a lot less scary than crashing the $8,000 beast that just emptied your bank account. As long as it still gets updates, swap out the worn props, give the batteries a once-over and let your archaic DJI drone be a kamikaze risk-taker or a solid spare.

Now that it's been replaced, its best job is practice, especially for new maneuvers or teaching someone else how to fly one. When you want to work on tight turns or low approaches, risk the geriatric version and spare your best drone. Leave the new one in the box for risky flights through heavy tree canopies or over water.

The old one also makes for a good spare in case the newbie runs out of juice or face-plants into a brick wall. Depending on your model, add-ons like the Sky Rigger make it a good fit for dropping bait when fishing.

Trading the drone or selling it is an obvious and simple option, but you can also part it out, either for future spare parts in your toolbox or to sell individually. There's a sizable market for specific drone parts, and as long as everything is in good working order, you won't have a problem finding buyers. Some parts can be repurposed for something entirely different, like security cameras or portable chargers.

For the airborne filmmakers out there, an older or budget DJI drone still holds up well in that regard. Say you want to record a low flight scene over water but are afraid of turning your drone into a submarine. Unless they've been wrecked a lot, older DJIs still fly steady lines and have stable cameras.

The cameras themselves aren't too shabby either. The Mavic 2 Pro and Air 2S shoot 4K video with D-Log and impressive dynamic range, and though newer drones add more digital stabilization, older ones still have physical gimbal motors that work surprisingly well.

Huge or important events deserve the highest-quality cameras you can afford to send skyward, but older DJI models are more than enough for property shots or planning projects without risking the newbie. They're also good for inspecting your roof or checking out the bat population hanging out at the top of a cedar tree. Drone mapping is an interesting and potentially lucrative side gig for your old drone as well.

Of course, you'll need more than just the drone, including mapping software and, for any paid work, an FAA Part 107 remote pilot certificate. You can even rent out your drone or offer your piloting services for special events. If you have a solid but older drone, why not make some money off it before you trade it in or sell it?

Hand the controller over to one of your kids or someone who has never flown a drone and is looking to get into the hobby. Yeah, it's a basic use case, but it'll feel much better if the noob crashes and burns the old drone and not the new one. Everybody interested in the hobby has to learn at some point. If you still have strong feelings toward your old drone, start in an open field, well away from trees and power lines. Keep the flight time short and don't let them try anything overly "clever."

Depending on how deep you're into the hobby, you can take the parts and work on a new build. DJI manufactures its drones with little in the way of interchangeability, but that doesn't stop you from repurposing the parts for a new drone. If you go this route, keep in mind that it requires a lot of time, tools and focused patience for tight, intricate work. You need at least a basic working knowledge of soldering, electronics and aerodynamics. Even if you're learning from scratch, it's a fun and rewarding journey from start to finish.

Lastly, you can use your DJI drone to map out yellow jacket, hornet, wasp and bee nests for exterminators. Make sure you're in a safe place when you do; locating those annoying nests and holes will make an exterminator's job much easier. Just know your drone may take a beating. None of the above stinging insects will throw out the welcome mat for a much larger, louder version of themselves.

#207. Divisions deepen between EU member states after tense budget summit

An EU leaders summit on the bloc's seven-year budget fell apart amid divisions over how to fund Ukraine. The budget proposal also includes a 3% tax on US tech companies, in a bid for the EU to generate additional funds.

EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.

Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.

There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.

"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.

The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.

Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."

Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.

Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.

In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).

"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."

Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.

"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.

Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.

Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.

They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.

In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.

The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.

The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.

But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.

"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.

There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.

The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.

EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."

Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.

"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."

Enache called the tax proposal "politically impossible."

EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.

#205. Why updating your iPhone can improve your CarPlay experience

Skipping iPhone updates can cost you new CarPlay features. Here's what you could be missing.

CarPlay is a great way to get all of your music, contacts and addresses on your car's infotainment system. But CarPlay isn't an app installed on your car. It runs straight from your iPhone, so the car usually doesn't have an "update CarPlay" option of its own. To update CarPlay, you need to update iOS.

CarPlay keeps working even if you don't update your phone, but you'll miss out on the new features, bug fixes and compatibility improvements. iOS 27, released September 14, added an audio mini-player, plus route sharing and video apps on supported cars. Apple says it also improves wireless CarPlay reliability and GPS accuracy. Here's how updating your iPhone can improve your CarPlay experience.

To update your iPhone, go to Settings > General > Software Update and check your iOS version. If a newer one is available, it will be waiting for you there. The latest version at the time of writing is iOS 27.2.1 (November 9). Phones still on iOS 26 will see a small iOS 26 update and the larger iOS 27 upgrade as separate options.

iOS 27 (September 14) added several new CarPlay features, including an audio mini-player, a progress bar in Now Playing, route sharing with the car's own screens, and apps for watching videos while the car is parked. The video apps and the route sharing option only work on cars where the automaker added support. Apple says iOS 27 also improves wireless CarPlay reliability and the accuracy of navigation heading and GPS.

iOS 27.2 (October 26) added even more options, including a Podcasts Home tab with New Episodes and Continue Playing in place of Up Next. Siri also got an upgrade and can now recall past conversations. Keep in mind that Siri needs an iPhone 15 Pro or later, so not every phone gets it.

If you skip every update Apple offers you, CarPlay will keep working as usual, with the features it already has. iOS 27 needs an iPhone 11 or later (or the second-generation iPhone SE), but Apple lists CarPlay as compatible with much older iPhones. Those phones still work but never get the new iOS 27 features.

If CarPlay is acting up, try updating your phone first. If that doesn't work, restart your phone and your car, then go to Settings > General > CarPlay, select your car, tap Forget This Car and set it up again. If that still doesn't work, try updating your car's stereo firmware. Apple lists this as the last troubleshooting step and points to the car's manual for more information.

#203. Should you repair or replace your PC's motherboard?

Hints to the declining health of your motherboard aren't subtle.

As the price of new PC components continues to rise, with seemingly no signs of relief in the immediate future, the prospect of replacing a part in your computer might be intimidating. If anything in your computer fails, the price of that potential part is likely going to be somewhat steep. When it comes to your motherboard, however, there's some leeway on when that may need to actually be replaced.

If you're lucky, you may be able to just outright repair a motherboard instead of buying a new one. In terms of PC parts, your motherboard ranks fairly high on the list of important items, so being able to repair a potentially failing board versus buying one certainly has distinct advantages.

Thankfully, hints to the declining health of your motherboard aren't subtle. The board sends out alarm bells about its current status rather frequently, and they're quite easy to identify once you understand what they are. Once you know these signs, and which ones point to a simple repair versus outright disaster, you'll be able to fully diagnose your next steps.

A standard motherboard of decent quality can last up to a rather generous ten years. But PC parts, as ever, are some of the most unpredictable pieces of hardware in the entire world. Inside a custom-built PC, the choice of a motherboard can often frame the entire identity of a build, so you may eventually find yourself in need of a full-blown replacement.

In some cases, the board's dying breaths are signaled by a POST failure. POST, or the power-on self-test, is what all motherboards do when you boot the PC. It checks the health and status of your components, and a POST failure is generally attributed to a piece of hardware not acting properly. When a failure to POST is accompanied by beeps or signals from your PC, however, that's when you'll need to worry.

Additionally, if you find that your PC is having issues reaching your operating system or you're getting hit with random "blue screens of death," it could be a sign that something has gone wrong either at a software level or even on the board itself. Damaged capacitors or even unruly thermal paste applications can lead to overheating, and thus internal board damage. RAM and PCIe slots going bad can be something of a killer, so replacing the motherboard may be your only choice in those situations.

On the other hand, replacing a board can sometimes come down to an upgrade that may be beneficial to you in the long run. If you haven't upgraded your board in a while, it can be quite useful to look into an update of some kind. While the higher-end boards will run your bill up, you can actually get pretty decent units of remarkable quality for a shockingly low price. Motherboards are fairly sturdy pieces of hardware, but replacing your old board with something that you want actually has more value than it seems. So even if your current motherboard is working OK, it may be worth looking into updating to newer hardware.

As your motherboard is made up of a lot of different parts that communicate with each other, it also has a lot of things that can go wrong with it. Capacitors, which supply voltage and current to the board's individual parts, can go belly up in a number of ways. If you have the means and skill with a soldering kit, it's entirely possible to put those skills to use in order to replace them. One piece of hardware that can help greatly in these situations is a multimeter, which can be used to test whether a fuse or power coil has burned out.

Additionally, if you happen to accidentally bend some of the pins on a CPU socket that has pins on the board itself, it's very doable to smooth them back into place, though it requires patience. Meanwhile, something as simple as a bad CMOS battery, which can cause limited to more severe issues, can be replaced within minutes. You may also benefit from something as simple as a cleaning or reapplying thermal paste to your CPU, but be aware that it can have some adverse impact on your board if not done properly. Each of these parts costs less than a standard cup of coffee, which makes the idea of doing the work yourself even more appealing.

Whether you repair or replace a motherboard is often determined by the severity of the issue, and in many cases, it's more beneficial to simply swap it out for a new one. Minor repairs like bad capacitors, a dead CMOS battery or even fixing slightly bent pins are incredibly common and easy. If your board has issues that interfere with your ability to use the machine, it's probably well past time for a replacement.

#201. 5 cool Amazon Echo Show features you shouldn't overlook

Amazon has a bunch of new smart devices coming, but some of the new features work on older devices, too.

In many owners' homes, mine included, an Echo Show spends most of its time serving as a very expensive kitchen clock. It shows the weather, cycles through a few photos and is occasionally used to set cooking timers or listen to the radio. It's a real shame, because that high-tech clock is also a touchscreen smart home hub, a video-calling camera, a Fire TV and a home monitor all at once — and some of its best features are buried a few menus deep.

Amazon returned the spotlight to its smart displays back in October with the announcement of the Echo Show 16. That's a $499.99 wall-mountable model with a 16-inch screen, switchable home screen layouts it calls Screen Styles, a 3D smart home map and a new way to organize your Alexa conversations. It was one of several new devices Amazon showed off at the end of October, including Echo Time, Alexa Photo Frame and more. But there's no need to go out and buy a new Echo Show to use what most of Amazon was demoing. Several of the features I've included here will work on older models, and a couple are on the way.

Alexa Home Map was by far the feature that got the most attention during Amazon's October event, and some might call it dystopian. It's essentially an interactive 3D model of your house that maps all your connected devices — lights, locks, thermostat, cameras — to where they are in your home, and you can tap on any device to control it. Lights, for example, will glow on the map in the color you've set them to, and if you've got Ring cameras outside, people moving around your property show up as animated figures. You can even rewind the last 24 hours across all your cameras by using the timeline feature.

But what many people don't realize is that owners of the older Echo Show 15 and 21 devices already have a 2D version. It's called Map View, and with Alexa+, you can open it straight from the smart home dashboard. You build the floor plan once in the Alexa app, which scans each room with its camera and sensors and turns the scans into a plan. Amazon first launched this feature back in 2023, and it requires a LiDAR-equipped iOS device to work, such as an iPhone 12 Pro or a fourth-gen iPad or later.

To set it up, open the Alexa app and go to Devices > Map View > Start Now and then walk your house room by room. Once that data is on your Echo Show, a single tap on a device will open a side panel with its controls, while a double tap will turn it on or off. It's also possible to filter the map so that it only shows lights or cameras, and switch between floors. Setting up Map View makes it much easier for guests or anyone else in the house to control devices when they don't know that the lamp in the corner is called "Living Room Plug 2." Amazon says the 3D Home Map will begin rolling out later this year on its larger Echo Show devices, as well as the Alexa and Ring apps.

Most people set up Alexa Routines focused around a voice command or a time of day, like "Alexa, good morning" or lights automatically turning off at 11PM. The camera-equipped Echo Shows can do something a lot more useful, though: start a Routine because someone walked into the room. Amazon gives the example of the kitchen lights turning on and Alexa reading out the weather when someone comes in first thing in the morning, but there's a lot more you can do to tailor it around your schedule.

You've got two options with Routines. Occupancy Routines activate when anyone is detected. Amazon says they work on the Echo Show 15, 10 (third-gen or newer), 8 (second-gen or newer) and some Echo speakers. The other type is Personal Presence Routines. These go a step further by using your Visual ID profile to recognize who walked in, so your Routine can play your tailored news briefing while your partner's can show their calendar. These personalized Routines work on the Echo Show 8 (second-gen and newer), Echo Show 10, the 2025 Echo Show 11, Echo Show 15 and Echo Show 21.

To use it, you'll need to set up a Visual ID first, which you can enroll in from your Echo display. Then, in the Alexa app, go to More > Routines and tap the plus button, select Add an Event and choose Presence Routine. You can then choose who to apply the Routine to, which Echo device does the watching and add the actions you want, like triggering a reminder at a set time and date or reading the latest news headlines. If the idea of a camera watching for you sounds a bit... too much, Amazon says all the processing to detect presence happens on the Echo Show and that it sends no images or video to the cloud.

If you've got one of the larger Echo Shows, then there's a full Fire TV hiding inside. Amazon brought Fire TV to the original Echo Show 15 as a free update in 2022, after finding that most owners were already using it to watch video. The refreshed Echo Show 15 and 21 both come with it built in and an Alexa Voice Remote in the box. Meanwhile, the new Echo Show 16 gets the full Fire TV interface, too. That means you don't just get Prime Video but also all the other popular streaming apps like Netflix, Disney+, YouTube and HBO Max.

However, the more useful trick is being able to move what you're watching between two different screens. Amazon essentially marketed the Echo Show 15 and 21 as the place to start a show while you're cooking, then send it to the living room Fire TV and finish it while you eat. With Alexa+, you can do more of that using your voice, such as by asking for a recommendation based on what you like, adding something to your watchlist, pulling up stats for the game you're watching or moving what's playing to a different TV. Streaming aside, the larger Echo Shows can open the full Amazon.com site, and I find that comparing a few options on a bigger screen before I click Buy Now works a lot better than squinting at my phone.

Until now, if you asked Alexa a question, the answer vanished from the Echo device the moment it finished. Sure, you can find your voice history in your Amazon account, but it's a pain to do. With Alexa+, Amazon has started saving those conversations as Cards, which are organized by topic in the Card Gallery and can be pinned so that the ones you use most stay at the top. If, for example, you spend your Saturday morning creating a shopping list with Alexa, it'll put everything into one Card you can come back to.

The answers themselves look a little different, too. Rather than showing a plain transcript of your conversation history, Alexa+ builds the response on screen as it goes. That means pulling in visuals, videos, calendar events and actions it can take for you. Amazon's example is shopping for a rain jacket, where Alexa might put together a chart comparing a few options, a list of things to look for, prices and links for each one. That's a lot closer to how you'd probably use a big screen in the kitchen, rather than reading a wall of text.

You're not being left behind if you don't plan on getting an Echo Show 16, though. Amazon says that Cards are also available in the Alexa app and on Alexa.com, so a conversation you start with your Echo Show can be picked up on your phone on the way to the store. Amazon hasn't confirmed when the Cards view itself will reach older Echo Shows, though.

All Echo Shows have a camera for video calls that most people don't really use for anything else. But if you turn on Home Monitoring, you can open a live feed from the display's camera while you're out, from the Alexa app on your phone or from another Echo Show, Fire TV or Fire tablet in the house. It's a super easy way to check in on the dog without having to buy a separate indoor camera.

On the Echo Show 15 and 21, that's a 13-megapixel wide-angle camera with auto-framing, but it doesn't record footage as a dedicated security camera would. Meanwhile, the Echo Show 16 is the first with night vision, and Amazon says its Visual ID can recognize you from up to 17 feet away. If you've also got Ring cameras, Alexa+ can pull them into the same screen and, with a Ring Premium Legacy (formerly Home Premium) subscription, summarize what your cameras have picked up.

Amazon also uses the Echo Show's big screen to show you ads. Not discreet ones, but full-screen sponsored ads. They began appearing on Echo Show in 2025, and Amazon told Tom's Guide that the devices are designed to show them when someone comes close. There's no ad-free option, which is a big part of why some owners have given up on Echo Show altogether.

#200. Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.

Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.

That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.

The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.)

Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail. Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#199. A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine shows early promise

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

China and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

The researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

It also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

They have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

#198. France seeks German man in Channel migrant boat probe

A German businessman is accused of supplying equipment to smugglers organizing migrant crossings from France to the United Kingdom. However, he can't face formal charges until he is extradited to France.

France has issued an arrest warrant for a German businessman as part of an investigation regarding the migrant deaths in the English Channel.

Joint investigation by several media outlets including French daily Le Monde and the BBC showed that Marvin R.* of MaRe Boote, managing director of a small firm in western German town Werne, is suspected of being one of the main suppliers of inflatable boats smugglers use to journey across the Channel.

According to the media reports, the 35-year-old businessman is accused of supplying smuggling gangs with inflatable boats, engines and life jackets worth hundreds of thousands of euros.

UK authorities estimated that boats or engines linked to MaRe Boote were responsible for three in every 10 detected crossings during the first four months of this year, the BBC and Le Monde reported.

The prosecutor in the northern French city of Lille, Samuel Finielz, confirmed late on Thursday that "five people had been arrested and a German national was briefly detained in his country."

According to Finielz, this is part of the investigation about Channel crossings and sinkings since May last year.

The five others are now held in pre-trial detention and were suspected of offenses including "assisting illegal entry and residence as part of an organized criminal group, involuntary manslaughter, involuntary injury and endangering the lives of others," Finielz told the media.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Lille authorities in May issued an arrest warrant against "the German national implicated in this case," he said, on charges of manslaughter and endangering the lives of others.

Marvin R. was arrested and released by German authorities and now required to appear before a French court before January, the prosecutor added.

The BBC wrote that Marvin R. is contesting extradition to France. He can not be formally charged until he is extradited to France, it noted.

Migrants frequently cross the English Channel from France to the United Kingdom in small rubber dinghy boats. It is a dangerous journey as the Channel is one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year and there have been many deaths.

#197. Car speakers rattling? Try these fixes before calling a mechanic

Check these common culprits before you go to the pros.

There you are, just singing along to your favorite tunes when you hear that awful noise. Rattling car speakers. Your mind probably wanders right to your bank account balance, because this is definitely going to cost you hundreds, if not thousands, of dollars for a new car audio system. Right?

Not so fast. Rattling car speakers, while extremely annoying, may not be the result of any catastrophic audio equipment failure or damage. It could actually be a simple fix. So, before you take your car to an audio specialist and have a new sound system installed, try to first determine the cause of the rattling. Then see if one of these easy solutions works for you.

Obviously, if components within the speakers are damaged, rattling can occur. But the culprits are often simply power and volume. If your speakers are using more power than the speaker cone can handle, the result is typically rattling and distortion. But not enough power, usually caused by a weak amplifier, can also cause distortion.

As far as volume is concerned, you probably already know that the higher the volume (especially if there's lots of bass), the more likely your car speakers are going to rattle. The reason? Science. Bass frequencies use a lot of power, and that causes more movement in the cones inside the speakers. That movement can cause loose components in the speaker to move against each other. Heavy bass also makes your car's door panels vibrate, in which case it may not be your speakers vibrating at all. But it's not just booming bass that can cause rattling issues. High volume creates excess heat in the speaker's voice coil, resulting in rattle-like distortion.

Debris finding its way into the speakers can also cause rattling if it comes into contact with moving speaker parts. And the cabinet that holds the speaker within the door panels or rear decks often vibrates with the music if the surfaces are poorly dampened — this creates a rattling sound that many people think is coming from the speakers themselves.

The rattling, especially if it occurs even at low volumes, could also be something as simple as loose mounting hardware. When the screws come loose, as a result of either poor installation or road vibration, rattling is common. Check to see if there is space between the speaker and its mounting surface. If so, tightening the screws should help. Also, try pressing the speaker panel when you hear distortion. If the distortion stops when you press it, it's likely just loose mounting hardware or noise from the cabinet.

With all these possibilities, the next thing to do is try to eliminate some of the causes and diagnose the origin of the rattling so you can determine whether it can be fixed at home or needs to be seen by a professional.

The first thing to focus on is finding out whether the speaker is simply rattling or if it's completely blown. If it's just rattling, it should be fixable. If it's blown, however, you're going to need a new speaker.

You can often tell if a speaker is blown simply by listening. For example, you'll hear distortion at any volume level, where rattling typically only happens at high volumes. Another thing to listen for is a missing frequency, like a lack of bass or no high frequency. This could be the result of a broken speaker.

If you determine that the speaker is not blown, it's time to start testing different tones and frequency ranges to identify the source of the rattling. Using test tones or the equalizer on your stereo's head unit, try out different frequency ranges to find the point where the rattling occurs. Rattling coming from low frequencies signals that the problem may involve bass-related components like subwoofers (if your vehicle has them) or bass response. If the rattling occurs during midrange frequencies, the culprit could be the door speakers. And if you notice the rattling when high frequencies are played, it might be smaller components like the tweeters.

Finally, use the eye and touch tests. Thoroughly check your speaker for any broken components; surrounds, voice coils and cones are typically the components that show visual damage. And if any of them are broken or damaged, it's time for a new speaker.

First, check the speaker wiring, especially if you've ever had work done on the speakers or have done any yourself. Sometimes the rattling can simply be reversed polarity, with the positive and negative terminals incorrectly connected. More often, however, wiring can become jarred loose from years of road vibration. You can test this by playing music and then lightly wiggling the speaker wires behind the head unit or where they come into the door. If the noise stops or gets worse when you move the wire, it's either a loose terminal or a break in the wire's insulation.

If you've diagnosed a power issue, there are a few fixes to try. If overpowering is the problem, start by reducing the gain on your amplifier and then slowly increasing it until you find the right balance. A multimeter can come in handy here, as it'll let you know whether you're going beyond the speakers' RMS power rating. If underpowering is the problem, you can either upgrade the amplifier or disconnect some speakers to cut down on the amp's load.

Test out your equalizer settings by resetting your EQ to zero across the board, then play music and gradually turn up the settings until you identify where the rattling begins. If you can find the frequency range where the rattling starts, you should be able to adjust your settings until the rattling stops.

If you think loose mounting hardware is the cause of the rattling, take off the speaker grilles and check to see whether any mounting screws are loose. Any trouble tightening them may require longer screws or new mounting holes. To minimize vibrations, you can also add a foam gasket between the mounting surface and the speaker.

Adding sound-deadening material like peel-and-stick butyl rubber mats with an aluminum foil backing to some of the flat metal surfaces on your car's door panels can also minimize resonance. Closed-cell foam decoupling sheets, weather stripping tape or foam speaker baffle rings placed around the speaker and along the panel edges also act as a cushion between vibrating pieces.

Ultimately, if these fixes don't help, there could be major damage to a speaker component, at which point replacement by a car audio specialist probably makes the most sense. But it's definitely worth giving these DIY fixes a shot before you drop big money on new speakers.

#195. European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment

“DART made a really, really large mess. However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess.”

Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.

Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.

But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.

“We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.”

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida. On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos. The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across.

Mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth.

“I would say we had two kinds of predictions: either we made a crater, or we reshaped the asteroid,” said Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator from Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France. “In fact, we did both because the crater is so large that the shape has changed. Therefore, we are in a sort of a transition between just cratering and global transformation, and we are still not sure how this can happen.”

Hera found Didymos, the larger of the two asteroids, spinning on its axis just as DART observed on final approach in 2022. Dimorphos is no longer so stable.

“As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit,” says Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist.

The Hera spacecraft will fly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos over the next six months to obtain more detailed observations. Hera will release two small sub-satellites to attempt landings on Dimorphos and collect data on the asteroid’s composition, internal structure, and mass.

Scientists will use this information to reconstruct the dynamics of DART’s impact four years ago and better understand how a future deflection mission might move an asteroid off a trajectory that actually threatens Earth. Near-Earth asteroids come in many shapes and sizes, with different densities and makeups, so knowledge of Dimorphos’s physical properties will anchor predictive computer models teaching scientists how best to deflect all types of asteroids.

“Once we understand, we have a breakthrough, which really solves planetary defense,” Michel said in an interview with Ars.

In its initial reconnaissance this month, Hera spotted hundreds of boulders surrounding the double asteroid. This was not entirely unexpected. A picture taken by the Hubble Space Telescope shortly after DART’s impact showed a cloud of material streaming behind Didymos and Dimorphos, but scientists were astonished by the extent of the debris swarm in Hera’s first images.

“As we approached Didymos and Dimorphos, we quickly realized the asteroids were not alone,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace in Toulouse, France. “In fact, they had a lot of company.”

An image released by ESA on Wednesday combines 11 long exposure frames from Hera’s hyperspectral camera. Image processors on the ground digitally removed the relatively bright Didymos and Dimorphos to reveal a panoply of dimmer streaks and dots, each of which is a rock fragment ranging in size from a football to a washing machine, Murdoch said.

“Hera came to visit two asteroids, and we found hundreds of companions,” Murdoch said.

One obvious explanation for the boulders is they were thrown off Dimorphos when DART slammed into it. But scientists cautioned they need more information before they can say that with surety. Hera is the first space mission to undertake a sustained study of an asteroid with its own moon. The debris around the two asteroids might be relics from the creation of Dimorphos some time in the ancient past.

“Hera will allow us to study that in more detail,” Murdoch said. “We really need to know more about these boulders and characterize them to understand if they’re linked to DART, if they’re linked to another process, and what the consequences might be for other asteroid systems in the Solar System.”

The boulder field will create challenges for navigating around the asteroids. In particular, the boulders are an added risk for the two small CubeSats Hera is supposed to deploy in January.

“We saw a couple of images that didn’t reassure me,” said Margherita Cardi, project manager for the Milani CubeSat. “There is a mix of excitement and panic.”

Claudia Balossi, spacecraft systems engineer for Hera’s other CubeSat, named Juventas, said her mission’s planned trajectory would take it right through the boulders as it moves within a couple of miles of the asteroids, then finally toward a landing attempt on Dimorphos, where it will measure the miniature world’s tenuous gravity field.

“We are right in the middle of it,” Balossi said. “The smallest ones are probably just as big as we are and the biggest ones are very big. In the worst case, a boulder will land on us. We will activate our gravimeter right away [if that happens],” Balossi joked.

The good news is the asteroids’ gravity is so weak that Hera, Milani, Juventas, and the hazards around them all move at snail-like speeds. Hera’s current trajectory takes it around the asteroids at a relative velocity of just a quarter-mile per hour, or about 12 centimeters per second. At that speed, there’s no danger of a sudden catastrophic hypervelocity collision between the spacecraft and the boulders lurking nearby.

Scientists have seen this at an asteroid before. NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft kicked up an estimated six tons of rock and dust when it gently moved in to collect a sample from an asteroid named Bennu in 2020. Low gravity and weak surface cohesion are a recipe for outsized effects.

“These types of bodies, because of their low gravity, have a very counterintuitive behavior,” Michel said. “Each time we interact with them, whether to take a sample or to make an impact, the response of the surface was not the one we predicted, simply because our intuition relies on what we experience every day on Earth. Even if the rules of physics are the same in the Universe, they express very differently depending on local attraction.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.
