#171. These settings can adjust your Samsung phone's display to your liking

Some of these will increase your battery life.

As one of the world's leading display manufacturers, even supplying screens to its biggest competitors, Samsung makes smartphones that are accordingly pixel-packed with display features. As in many other areas, Samsung lets users take the initiative to customize their smartphone displays, but it doesn't do a very good job of making sure you know those options exist.

Maybe you've found that your expensive Galaxy flagship seems to have a lower resolution than the spec sheet led you to believe, or that it seems a bit less responsive to your swipes than an iPhone 18 Pro. That's because your resolution and refresh rate are artificially capped by Samsung. Maybe your display isn't very bright. Maybe it's too bright. And have you ever wished you could leave the screen off without the whole phone going into sleep mode? Samsung has solutions for all of these and more baked into the past several versions of its One UI Android skin.

These features were tested on a Galaxy S23 Ultra, S25 Ultra and S26 Ultra running the latest One UI 9 software, along with both Galaxy Tab S9 and Tab S10 Ultra tablets running the previous One UI 8.5. Some features cannot be immediately confirmed to work on devices older than the Galaxy S23 Ultra but may still be available on some of them. Only one feature we covered, Super HDR, is unavailable on the S23 Ultra, since it was added with the S24 series and works at a hardware level.

If you own one of Samsung's higher-end Galaxy phones such as a Galaxy S26+, S26 Ultra or Fold Z 8, your phone comes out of the box set to 1080p but can actually go a lot higher. The same is true of the screen's refresh rate, which can reach 120Hz for smooth scrolling and gaming but arrives from the factory set to just half that. To remedy this, you can open Settings by swiping down from the top right corner of the display and then tapping the gear icon in that same corner. Select Display, then Motion smoothness and set the screen to Adaptive, then press Apply. Go back to Display settings, tap Screen resolution and select the rightmost option with the highest resolution your device offers, then tap Apply.

Both settings will consume extra battery, so be sure you're willing to make that trade-off beforehand if you care about improving your phone's battery life.

One more display setting worth tweaking in Display settings is Screen mode. This lets you choose how colors appear onscreen. Samsung defaults to Vivid mode, which cranks up sharpness and saturation, making content onscreen look more candy-coated and vibrant. However, this comes at the cost of accuracy. If you want a more true-to-life image, you should switch to Natural. If you prefer Vivid, you can customize things a bit further. With Vivid selected, newer Galaxy devices show a white balance slider that lets you make the image warmer (shifting toward reds and yellows) or cooler (shifting toward blues). You can also tap Advanced settings to find individual red, green and blue sliders for more granular cast compensation, as well as a Vividness slider that can crank the saturation even higher.

Modern OLED displays like those found in Samsung's flagship Galaxy phones and tablets are reaching increasing levels of brightness, but OLED struggles with brightness compared to other panel technologies. Meanwhile, in pitch-black conditions such as when you're reading in bed, even the dimmest brightness setting can be too much for some users (or might bother the person sleeping next to you). Samsung seems to understand this, and One UI includes both an extra bright and extra dim setting to compensate.

In direct sunlight, your Galaxy phone will flex past its normal top brightness level to make sure the screen remains visible, but this special sunlight mode otherwise stays dormant. You can enable it manually, however. First, you need to turn off automatic dimming by pulling down the Quick Panel from the top right corner of the display and holding down on the brightness slider to access brightness settings, then toggling off Adaptive brightness. Once you do, a new toggle for Extra brightness will appear. When enabled, the screen will get brighter than it could be with the slider all the way at max brightness.

If you want the screen to be extra dark, that's also possible, but you'll need to go into the Accessibility section of the Settings app, then tap Vision enhancements. You can toggle on Extra dim from here, or tap on the setting to configure it further. If you use it frequently, toggle on the Extra dim shortcut option, which will add a toggle to your Quick Panel for instant bedtime reading sessions.

The screen timeout on your Samsung Galaxy smartphone ensures you won't accidentally drain the battery by leaving the screen on indefinitely. When you turn your screen off, you're actually putting the phone into sleep mode. Nonessential processes are paused, radios scan less frequently and the CPU relaxes in frequency. Additionally, your screen itself takes a lot of power to run, especially at high refresh rates and resolutions, so turning it off conserves even more power.

But sometimes you need the display to remain on regardless, and sometimes you need your phone to run internally at full power even when the screen is off. Samsung has ways to accomplish both without changing your settings indefinitely, but to take advantage of them, you'll need to download the Good Lock application from the Galaxy Store or Google Play and install the Display Assistant module inside of it. This unlocks One UI features you won't get on other Android phones.

Once Display Assistant is installed, you'll find two new toggles in your Quick Panel (accessed by swiping down from the top right-hand corner of the screen). Keep screen on is represented by a downward-facing lamp icon and is pretty self-explanatory. When toggled on, the screen will remain awake for half an hour, at which point you will be prompted to extend it another half hour. The other new toggle you can add to the Quick Panel is Screen Curtain, which turns the screen off but keeps the phone running as though it were still on. This comes in handy during situations where you need the phone to keep running a task  — for example, exporting a long 4K video edit  — but you don't want the screen to drain battery unnecessarily while it does so.

If you're like most people, you spend more time on your phone than you care to admit. Whether you've got real work to attend to or simply get caught up doomscrolling (it happens to the best of us), all that screen time can cause eyestrain that leads to headaches and fatigue. Most devices now include a blue light filter for that reason. Though recent research suggests reducing blue light may not be as effective as once believed for reducing eyestrain or maintaining sleep hygiene, some people do find it more comfortable to filter out some of the dominant blue hues in modern displays.

Samsung's blue light filter can be found in the Quick Panel, where it is called Eye comfort shield. Alternatively, you can go to the Display section of the Settings app to find the same toggle. You can further tune the blue light filter by holding down on the Quick Panel toggle or tapping the option in Settings. You can choose between Adaptive and Custom temperature modes, set a schedule to enable the filter only at certain times of day and choose how intense the effect is when enabled.

Another related Galaxy display feature helps to make images look consistent in different lighting conditions. The lighting around you can influence how you perceive content on a display, so the Adaptive Color Tone feature adjusts the screen's color temperature and brightness based on your environment. In theory, this helps you see your display more comfortably, but opinions are mixed. Some users report that it makes their screen feel more natural, while others have the opposite reaction. To try it for yourself, open the Quick Panel and hold down on the display brightness slider, then toggle on Adaptive color tone.

Viewing media on flagship Samsung phones is a visual treat thanks to the company's vivid OLED displays. Unless you own a very expensive OLED TV or monitor, there's a good chance your Samsung Galaxy phone has the best display in your home. But Samsung has added in a couple of features to make photos and videos even better. Both of them are somewhat counterintuitively hidden in the Advanced features section of the Settings app.

Video brightness will crank up the display's luminance and vibrance while watching local or streamed video from supported apps, toggleable per app. Our test devices showed support from the most common apps, including Netflix, Disney+, TikTok and YouTube, as well as Samsung's built-in video player and other local players like VLC. This likely means you're getting a less natural image, but it does make videos a lot punchier in bright environments.

Super HDR is another feature that enhances media by reading HDR data stored inside the SDR version of photos. It is based on Google's Ultra HDR format. HDR files look better because they balance shadows and highlights, but they need 10-bit color and can therefore break compatibility on older screens. Super HDR encodes a gain map  — the data in an HDR file that tells it how to render brightness in different parts of an image  — into the standard version of the file when you take a photo on a Galaxy phone or other phones like recent Pixels that support Google Ultra HDR. Samsung even partnered with Instagram to make Super HDR work in that app, too, allowing you to share and view HDR content in your Stories and grid posts.

#169. 5 Android Auto navigation apps you could be using instead of Google Maps

Google Maps works just fine, but if you want something different that works with Android Auto, there are plenty of options.

Sometimes, Google Maps won't do for driving in certain cities. It might work brilliantly for driving in New York City, for instance, but poorly in another part of the world. User numbers can also make a difference: more drivers using a crowdsourced navigation app can help improve its routing, as with Waze. Or maybe you're looking for a different app because you don't trust Google with your driving info. Or you might simply prefer how another app looks and works more than Google Maps. At the end of the day, that's exactly what matters most.

Waze built its reputation on community-powered traffic data and that continues to be its biggest draw. There are tons of reports from drivers about accidents, speed traps, police presence, road closures and real-time traffic jams. If you were avoiding Google Maps because you don't want all your data in Google's hands, then you're out of luck because Waze is owned by the tech giant. Still, there's no denying that there are some benefits to this, because the app uses Gemini-powered Conversational Reporting. This way, you can speak naturally about what you saw rather than take your eyes off the road to report an issue.

Waze also provides a cool feature called personalized navigation, which suggests routes based on your past trips, and a less chatty mode that trims down voice prompts while keeping essential turn alerts intact. Spend five minutes exploring the hidden features every Waze user should know about, and you will see you can change a ton of things, from how your car shows up on the map to the voice guiding you. Or maybe you want Christina Aguilera to tell you when to turn left, or you want to hear dad jokes while you drive. It's all in there.

You should know, however, that Waze doesn't really support offline navigation. An already-loaded route may keep working if you briefly lose data, but you can't download offline maps. You might also find the screen to be cluttered with alerts popping up constantly, which can be annoying if your car's infotainment screen is on the smaller side.

Here WeGo takes a different approach to leading you places, leaning on frequently updated maps and decent global coverage rather than Waze-style community reports. It works with Android Auto for turn-by-turn navigation and features tons of business listings. You can also search for various other items nearby, like ATMs and pharmacies. Finding a gas station or a restaurant while you're driving somewhere will work well enough that you won't have to switch apps.

Offline maps are available for many countries; you can go completely offline on your travels once you've downloaded the maps, which is helpful if you're going to cross a border and perhaps face higher data costs. It's also ideal to use for areas with patchy mobile coverage. While Google Maps' chatbot can find appointments and call to book them for you, Here WeGo has a simpler appeal. This isn't going to be the best app to use if you want to discover new places, but it will take you to your destination just fine — with fewer distractions.

TomTom has been making GPS devices for decades, so naturally, its mobile app is a top contender as a Google Maps alternative for Android Auto. It's the same no-frills, distraction-free design, so you can focus on driving. If you find Google Maps too busy on your car's screen, TomTom's simpler interface might be enough reason to switch. You can also change your route if you need to and mark various issues like speed traps and closed roads. One of its better features is that when you choose a place you need to visit, the app lets you search for nearby parking. That's particularly handy when you're driving to a location you're unfamiliar with, so you don't have to go around the block a dozen times just to find available spots.

TomTom (formerly AmiGO) itself is free, but drivers who want more, like offline navigation, can pay for TomTom GO Expert. That one's built for truck drivers and other professionals, with features like routes tailored to a vehicle's height and weight, but you can definitely use it too if you really want.

MapQuest is another name that's been around since well before smartphones were a thing, and it's managed to stay relevant by adapting to modern driving habits. You can easily plan your route with the app, but it does come with the caveat that it's not a tool available worldwide. As long as you're driving in the United States or Canada, you're good to go. MapQuest gained Android Auto support in 2026, so you can finally take the app to the big(ger) screen in your car.

The MapQuest mobile app provides a more traditional navigation experience, with alternate routes and settings to avoid highways and toll roads, and even recently gained support for real-time reporting. You can plan a route with multiple stops too, which is handy if you're running errands or have a few places to visit on a road trip. You can also choose a starting point other than your current location, so you don't have to wait until you're ready to leave to work out a route. So if you've been using MapQuest for years and prefer how it handles route planning, the addition of Android Auto support means you can stick with it instead of switching to Google Maps the next time you get in your car.

Magic Earth comes with support for offline maps so you can navigate without depending on an internet connection. It also offers both 2D and 3D navigation views, giving you some extra flexibility in how the map looks.

The app used to be free to use, but these days it offers a freemium model. Basic navigation is free, but offline maps and real-time traffic info require a yearly subscription. Unfortunately, if you want to use this app with Android Auto, you'll need to pay $21.19 a year for the subscription. Thankfully, you can try the full version of the app for free for 14 days before deciding whether or not it's the right choice for you as a Google Maps alternative on Android Auto.

#166. How you can spot and avoid scam ads on social media

Convincing fake stores and AI-generated celebrity endorsements are making scam ads harder to recognize.

Imagine stumbling upon a Facebook ad for a jacket that's $300 under normal circumstances, going for a mere $39. With high-quality images and logos you recognize, plus a ticking clock to pressure you into buying within a short timeframe, these ads are often effective at getting you to act without thinking it through. But in most cases, that "bargain" is you handing over money to a fraudster.

Many people have fallen victim to scam ads on social media, some of which direct people to make a purchase from an external website. People reported losing over $95 million as a result of such purchases in 2025. Reported losses from all types of scams beginning on social media totaled $2.1 billion in the same year.

They may appear to be run by well-known and reputable businesses, sell nonexistent goods or feature fake celebrity endorsements (some created using AI). Many will direct you to a fake website, while others seek as many of your details as possible. As with most places online, having the word Sponsored simply means a fee has been paid to display the ad, so you need to investigate more to see whether it's legitimate.

Don't assume a phony site will be of poor quality and full of typos. Many scam ads will copy logos, images and their general look from the pages of well-known stores. Add large reductions with an offer counting down to "end of day", and they can be very convincing.

As recently as February 2026, Meta sued a Vietnam-based advertiser over a range of products purportedly available at reduced prices, including those of Longchamp. Shoppers completed a survey before reaching a site asking for credit card details. Meta said products were not delivered, but unauthorized recurring charges were made.

In separate cases, advertisers used manipulated images and voices of celebrities appearing to recommend healthcare products or lure victims into investment groups. With AI getting this good, classic giveaways like poor-quality images or awkward voiceovers aren't as common now.

The number of people affected by the Longchamp-style offers hasn't been disclosed. However, these are all good examples of how having the right logo and images, a well-produced clip with a celebrity or other recognizable features doesn't mean the source can be trusted.

As a general rule, it's best to avoid clicking through to any website. Instead, type the name of the shop or store into a new tab and go directly to their homepage. This will help you avoid impersonator sites, though it's still possible to fall for a "discount" page that isn't claiming to be a well-known brand if you're not careful.

Look carefully at the URL, which may have additional or different words, spelling or domain ending to impersonate a genuine site. Try Googling the company name and "scam", "fraud" and similar words, and reading others' comments and experiences. Many fraudulent sites will use stock images or photos lifted from other companies, so it can also be worthwhile to do a reverse image search.

Don't assume that the presence of a padlock icon or "HTTPS" at the start of the URL means the company is reputable. HTTPS only encrypts your connection to the site, and scammers can use it too. A secure connection to a fraudulent site doesn't protect you from falling for it.

It's also useful to pause for a moment and apply some common sense. Always remember the old "too good to be true" line: luxury brands are not going to suddenly offer their goods at 80 percent off when the prestige is their main selling point.

If possible, you should always pay with a credit card (or wallet like PayPal) when buying from an unknown website, as that gives you more protection if you need to dispute any transactions. If you're asked to pay using unusual methods like gift cards or money transfers, you're almost certainly dealing with a scam. Gift card payments are a frequent tactic of scammers; legitimate companies won't ask you to pay with them.

Naturally, none of the above will be totally reliable indicators on their own every time. Still, it's well worth taking a short time to research a company before purchasing from them, rather than trying to get a refund or have a problem resolved for many weeks afterwards.

In case you do open a shady website, don't enter your details or download any files. Double-check that nothing was downloaded, and decline any prompts to download programs. If something did get downloaded, don't open it. Delete it, then update and run an anti-malware scanner to make sure all is OK.

Entered a password or other details already? You should change those passwords, along with those for any other sites where you use the same password. If you've entered payment details, even if you didn't finish checking out, you should notify your bank or credit card company, explain what happened and ask them to prevent further payments. You can also ask them to reclaim any payments you made to the scam company.

Meta's page on fraudulent ads has links to report scam ads on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. TikTok's support also explains how to report an ad on that platform. Even after a report, you might see others like it, so keep your guard up.

It's also useful to take screenshots of the ad. Keep the URL of the website and details of any payments made, if they happened. You can report fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

#165. Spain's Sanchez makes final appeal to voters before election

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told people to turn out in large numbers so the country does not go "backwards." Polls suggest an end to his eight-year leftist leadership of Spain.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday hit the campaign trail one last time before Spaniards head to the polls on Sunday, telling people to "vote, vote, vote" to make sure the country doesn't go "backwards."

Opinion polls point to a change in government, with the conservative People's Party (PP) slated to come out on top, bringing an end to Sanchez's eight years of leftist leadership.

Spain's general election this Sunday is also crucial because it kicks off a round of elections on the continent and because it is yet another test of the region's shift to the right.

The PP would potentially have to rely on support from the far-right anti-immigration Vox party to form the next government in Spain.

There's also a chance that the election ends in a hung parliament, with neither the right-wing coalition nor the left bloc securing a majority.

Sanchez has so far campaigned on a platform of having boosted the Spanish economy when its European Union partners were struggling.

He has pointed to his policies of having increased the minimum wage and having lifted pensions in line with inflation.

But people are frustrated that the cost of living has soared and that they're not able to enjoy the fruits of economic growth, with many unable to leave their parents' house because of very high rental prices.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sanchez said during his final rally in Madrid that the "elections are about moving Spain forward, not moving it backwards."

He doubled down on an attempt to appeal to left-leaning voters, telling them that a right coalition government, with far-right members in parliament, would reverse the years of social progress and gut public services.

Oscar-winning Spanish film director Pedro Almodovar was also at the rally this evening.

Sanchez wore a red T-shirt that said "the power of the people," telling people that a "progressive majority is within our reach."

Sanchez has also become the standard-bearer for Europeans frustrated with the Trump administration.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has said that he wants to maintain good relations with US President Donald Trump, dismissed Sanchez's campaign of "fear."

Feijoo won the most seats during elections in 2023, but he was not able to form a government.

"And when a government has nothing to offer but fear, it means it has nothing else left to offer," he told supporters at his campaign finale in the southern city of Seville.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," said Feijoo, who built his career running central public bodies and the northwestern Galicia region.

He has advocated for tough immigration policies and stronger border management.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the Vox party, favors a much tougher approach, with his party having advocated for mass deportations.

Addressing a closing rally at a bullring in the eastern city of Valencia, Abascal told supporters not to "vote out of fear. Vote with courage."

"What we are up against is a criminal mafia led by a ruthless boss, a liar," he said, referring to the corruption scandals that have surrounded Sanchez and his government.

#164. Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister said in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has said he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

#162. 2026 Kindle Paperwhite review: Page-turn buttons are back, for a price

Kindles are getting costlier faster than they’re getting better.

Supply pressures, shortages, and inflation have pushed tech prices relentlessly upward over the last half-decade, and even basic gadgets haven’t been immune. That’s why you can spend $385 on a Raspberry Pi, or why the cheapest Amazon Kindle in 2026 costs more than the midrange one from a few years ago. “New thing, better features, same price” used to be a reliable formula, but now you’re lucky if you can get the same thing for barely more than before.

The 2024 Kindles all came with small price increases, but the 2026 models make them look like stellar deals. The $160 Kindle Paperwhite from two years ago wipes the floor with this year’s $150 Kindle in just about every conceivable way, from screen size to front light quality to waterproofing—something to consider if you’re choosing between a used or refurbished Paperwhite and one of these new models.

The flagship of the now five-model-large monochrome Kindle family is the $250 2026 Paperwhite Signature Edition, which takes the core specs of the new $200 Paperwhite and puts it in a sturdy iPad-esque aluminum case instead of the typical plastic.

It’s an exceptionally nice reader, and if you’re down with paying even more for it, longtime page-turn button holdouts can recover their precious buttons while still getting the benefits of new, fast Kindle hardware. With the exception of one regression—wireless charging, a feature of the 2024 Signature Edition that has been removed here—it’s the fastest and nicest Kindle you can get. It’s mostly the value, or lack thereof, that leaves a bad taste in one’s mouth.

Unlike the 2021 or 2024 Kindle Paperwhite updates, the 2026 Paperwhite doesn’t include any notable screen or lighting upgrades. Anyone upgrading from a two- or three-generation-old version of the hardware will still get an upgrade, but the 2026 Paperwhite isn’t doing a ton to push the category forward. And while speed increases were front-and-center in Amazon’s promotional material for the 2024 Paperwhite, Amazon isn’t highlighting any particular gains for this year’s Paperwhite (the base Kindle does apparently open books 30 percent faster than the previous-generation Kindle, though).

But the Paperwhite and this year’s basic Kindle both make a couple of tweaks worth mentioning that don’t really show up on a spec sheet. One is that the device’s power button moves from the bottom edge to the top-right edge, a small change I appreciate because I’ve accidentally pressed the bottom-mounted power button all the times I’ve tried to set the Kindle on the edge of something. The other is that the devices now have user-replaceable batteries, a change made in part to comply with right-to-repair regulations going into effect in some countries.

Whether you’re buying the standard plastic-backed Paperwhite or the aluminum Signature Edition, you’re still getting a 7-inch 300 PPI screen with a front light that can adjust its color temperature as well as its brightness, which I find makes the Paperwhite easier on the eyes than the harsher, more bluish-tinted front light on older Kindles and the basic 2026 Kindle. The plastic Paperwhite is a smidge lighter than the 2024 version, and the Signature Edition is a little heavier (thanks in part to the aluminum casing), though not by a lot in either direction.

Whether it’s faster than the 2024 Paperwhite or not, the snappy and fluid performance I observed while using that device is definitely present in this one. The E-Ink screen still puts a cap on exactly how fluid and responsive the device can feel, but you rarely feel the big gap between your touch input and the device responding to that input like you can on most older Kindles. (I tried repeatedly to run the old Google Octane 2.0 benchmark I used to get a sense of the 2024 Paperwhite’s relative performance, but it could never complete a run in either the 2026 Kindle or the 2026 Paperwhite’s browser, for whatever reason).

I didn’t spend as much time with it, but I did test the basic 6-inch Kindle alongside the Paperwhite Signature Edition.

Overall, I like the updated look and feel of the redesigned Kindle, particularly the fact that the screen and bezel are now flush, as the last few Paperwhites have been. And despite using the same 6-inch screen size as older Paperwhites, Amazon has significantly shrunk the overall size and weight of the device. It doesn’t quite look like a “Kindle mini” next to the current Paperwhite, but it’s not far off.

But you’re still getting less for your money than you were a few years ago. If you compare the 2026 Kindle to the 2024 or 2022 model, and you ignore what each one of those devices cost to buy, it looks like slow and steady improvement. But the fact is that you can pay $150 for this Kindle and lose important features, like the warm light and waterproofing, that Amazon offered in the 2021 Paperwhite for just $140 back in 2021.

That’s just the reality of buying technology right now. “Get more for the same money” is out. Now if you want more, you have to pay more.

The new Paperwhite Signature Edition’s biggest upgrade, should you choose to pay for it, is the addition of page-turn buttons. Page-turn buttons by proxy, at least.

The Signature Edition adds iPad-style copper contacts on the back, and for another $80 (on top of the $250 you’ll pay for the Kindle) you can buy a Kindle Page Turn Cover in various colors that connects to those contacts with pogo pins. It’s the cover that adds the buttons. Amazon also offers a $60 charging stand that uses the pins, the closest equivalent for the now-removed wireless charging feature.

The cover really does make the new Paperwhite look and feel a bit more like a Frankenstein Kindle Oasis, right down to the asymmetrical edge that the button area adds. And the page-turn buttons themselves feel good and work well. The physical feedback from clicky buttons and the Kindle’s overall responsiveness both make page turns feel nearly instantaneous when you press it to turn a single page. Clicking the buttons quickly to turn multiple pages still gets bogged down a little.

Functionally, the worst things I can say about the Page Turn Cover are that it adds to the reader’s size and weight, and the power button doesn’t feel nearly as good as the page-turn buttons. The case’s “button” is basically a little plastic nub that pushes in the device’s actual built-in power button. At least with the hardware I bought, the case’s button feels like it can’t consistently reach the device button, which means it wasn’t always reliable. This is partly moot because opening and closing the cover also wakes and sleeps the device.

Amazon offers one cheaper option for every other Kindle that can run the newest version of the Kindle operating system: a $35 remote control-style Kindle Click. As a completely separate accessory you have to hold or rest on something in order to use, I don’t find this to be a particularly compelling solution to the “no buttons” problem. But it’s also the only version of “clickable buttons” that Amazon offers for less than $330. It is what it is.

The Kindle Click requires a Kindle running version 5.20.1.0.2 or later of the Kindle operating system. Currently, that version only runs on the 2024 and 2026 Kindles, plus 2022’s Kindle Scribe. It seems as though Amazon has gotten stingier with long-tail Kindle OS updates than it was in 2024, when all Kindles going back to 2018 could run the same software. The 2018 Kindles currently top out at 5.18, while the other 2021/22 Kindles stop at 5.19.

The last reader Amazon offered with page-turn buttons was 2019’s $249 Kindle Oasis, which was dinged pretty much across the board for being “expensive.” Today’s Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition will cost you just as much, but charge you $80 extra for the case and buttons. It’s a nicer reader in some important ways, most notably its USB-C port and much-improved performance. But that’s still a pretty substantial increase for anyone with an aging Oasis they’d like to replace with a Paperwhite-plus-case.

That’s my response to the new Paperwhite and to all of this year’s Kindle releases in a nutshell. They are nice, but they’re so much more expensive than Kindles have been in the very recent past that it’s hard to feel very enthusiastic about them. The basic Kindle-versus-old-Paperwhite comparison is the one that’s the most frustrating—the Kindle has picked up Paperwhite-style pricing more quickly than it has added Paperwhite features.

Hopefully we’ll see third-party accessory makers figure out support for their own pogo-pinned accessories, to bring the pricing down just a little bit. Otherwise, if you don’t need or want buttons, the best way to find a good deal on a Kindle is probably to buy an old one—the 2024 Paperwhite is $130 right now, and you might want to get it while the getting’s good.

#159. The Alexa Photo Frame is the Echo Show without the bits you hate

An Alexa speaker with a screen that only shows your best photos? This is the smart display we’ve been asking for.

I have to face facts: I’m a digital hoarder. My son graduated high school this year, and to mark the occasion, I made him a scrapbook of his 12 years of school. He loved it, but one reaction surprised me: He said he’d never seen most of these photos. Unlike my childhood — documented in photo albums sitting on shelves for anyone to browse — the photographic evidence of my son’s childhood is sitting on my phone. Cue the mom-guilt.

While a few photos are framed around our house, my phone holds thousands of pictures of my son that he’s never seen. And that just feels wrong. The solution to this — getting photos off your phone and into your home — is the pitch behind Amazon’s newest gadget, the Alexa Photo Frame, which starts at $199.99.

Alexa is very good at curating your photosOnly shows photos: no adsSemi-matte, anti-glare screen displays photos beautifullyIt’s a full Alexa speaker

Requires Amazon Photos; no Google Photos supportPrime or Alexa Plus sub needed for Alexa curationLandscape only, no videoSpeakers are weak for musicAs expensive as an Echo Show 8

A smart digital photo frame that uses AI to surface your best photos automatically, the Frame is also an Alexa smart speaker. It seems Amazon has finally made the product its users have been asking for: a smart speaker that shows pictures — nothing more, nothing less. No rotating screen serving up a random smorgasbord of Alexa suggestions, weather, and news. No camera. And, best of all, no display ads. The only real question is, what took so long?

This feels like Amazon’s apology to customers who just wanted a goddamn digital photo frame

For years, Amazon’s Echo Show smart displays did a nice job displaying photos, but I couldn’t ever have them display only photos; there was always some rotating content showing Alexa suggestions or other cruft. In 2023, the company launched a more expensive dedicated photos edition of the Echo Show 8, but quickly discontinued it. Then, last year, Echo Shows started regularly showing full-screen display ads for motor oil and recliners between my family photos — and I quickly banished them to little-seen corners of my home.

The Alexa Photo Frame feels a bit like Amazon’s apology to customers who just wanted a goddamn digital photo frame — albeit an expensive one. The Frame does exactly what I wanted the Shows to do with photos, without showing anything else.

One word of caution: while it only shows photos today, the Frame’s 10-inch touchscreen is functionally the same as the Echo Shows, meaning nothing is stopping Amazon from adding ads down the line — which is what happened with the Shows. For now, Amazon has said the device only shows photos and does not display ads. In my three weeks of testing, that’s all it’s shown, and it’s done a nice job thanks to its AI-powered photo curation feature.

As a dedicated photo device, the Alexa Photo Frame is great. Photos look lovely on its anti-glare 1280 x 800, 16:10 aspect ratio screen, and the AI-powered photo selection does the hard work of curating your photos.

My favorite feature is the Daily Memories collection, the Frame’s default album, which pulls up pictures from this time in past years. All week I’ve been seeing past Thanksgiving celebrations and shots of my now-teenage kids sitting on Santa’s lap as toddlers. It’s been genuinely delightful.

The catch is you have to use Amazon Photos. Unlike other smart frames, it has no option to import directly from Google Photos or Apple’s iCloud, where your photos most likely live. If you pay for Amazon Prime, though, Amazon Photos offers free unlimited storage, and I could import my iPhone’s photo library just by opening the app and turning on automatic backup. It took a little over a day to back up my 100,000-plus photo library.

When the Frame shows vertical images, instead of cropping them or adding black bars as some frames do, it uses AI to pair them with similar pictures: my daughter Rollerblading alongside my son playing tennis; my daughter on the beach next to a shot of her playing in the snow; my son cuddling our dog next to one of him snuggling with our cat. It does a good job of pairing similar images, and I especially like when it serves up then-and-now pictures; it’s fun to see baby pictures next to shots of my grown-up kids.

Amazon says Alexa uses a combination of faces, time, and context to sort photos for you. It looks for smiles and good lighting while skipping screenshots and receipts, and also that close-up of the mole on your shoulder. Daily Memories is my favorite, but you can choose from auto-updating collections of specific people (not pets, sadly), create albums with specific images, and have multiple collections rotating at once. You can also invite family and friends to add their photos to the Frame.

The Frame is an Alexa smart speaker, and the on-board voice assistant can answer questions about your photos. When a picture of my kids in face masks visiting Santa popped up, I asked Alexa what year it was, and it answered correctly: “2021.” Then I asked to see more photos from that day, and it pulled up all the images from our visit and a slideshow play button — this would be a neat way to show off your holiday snaps when friends visit. You can also ask it for more specific requests: “Show me all the photos of my son playing tennis” or “Show me all the photos of my daughter playing bass.”

Digital photo frames I’ve used from Aura and Skylight rely more heavily on you fiddling with an app to add new pictures. Amazon’s special sauce is that once set up, it’s largely hands-free. Of course, Google has done this with its Nest Hub smart displays for years, and they have long been my favorite digital photo frames. But Nest Hub’s hardware is aging, and its algorithms aren’t as good (I have definitely seen some mole shots). The Alexa Photo Frame’s semi-matte screen also displays photos better with less glare. However, the Frame’s screen isn’t as good as the $229 Aura Aspen, with its higher 1600 x 1200 resolution and clever 4:3 aspect ratio that displays both horizontal and portrait images beautifully.

Along with the Frame’s white mat and actual frame (in black or wood), it looks more like a photo frame and less like a piece of tech than an Echo Show or Nest Hub. Don’t get me wrong: The Frame is unmistakably a screen, but like all digital photo frames, its benefit over a regular photo frame is fresh images every few seconds, minutes, hours, or once a day.

I tested the walnut model, which costs an extra $30; there’s also a birch model and the cheaper black option. It’s very solid and well-made. A light sensor adjusts the display based on ambient light (with the option to shut it off completely in a dark room). It has four microphones and a pair of stereo speakers for Alexa, plus a physical mute button to turn the voice assistant off and volume buttons. Unlike Aura or Skylight frames, it doesn’t play video or Live Photos, only static images, but it has a unique feature that lets you add a voice note to a photo that plays when you tap on it. I didn’t find much use for this personally, but Amazon bills this as a gifting feature, since it can play a message when the recipient sets it up. Probably a good option for the grandparents.

The other feature the Frame has over the competition is that it is a full-fledged Alexa Plus speaker and can do everything an Echo Dot can, including controlling your smart home, setting timers and alarms, and booking you a table at a local restaurant. Unlike an Echo Show, it doesn’t use its display to show information, just photos. The Frame’s built-in speaker is fine for podcasts and radio — a step up from your iPhone speakers, but not a big one. For music, pairing it with an Echo or a Bluetooth speaker in the Alexa app is the way to go.

If it could display a clock over the photos, like Apple’s HomeView smart display, it would make a great bedside table device, because there’s no camera and the screen goes totally black at night, so it won’t disturb you. But it really belongs in a living room where everyone can see all the photos that have been stuck on your phone for years.

Compared to the competition, Alexa adds real value here. As much as I love the Aura Aspen that I reviewed last year, my husband regularly complained that he was bored of the photos because I kept forgetting to add new ones to the album. My son came home from college this weekend and said the exact same thing about the Skylight on our wall. Now, this is user error, and if I were more proactive about updating those devices, it wouldn’t be an issue. But with the Frame it’s really nice not to have to think about it and still get fresh pictures.

However, Aura is completely subscription-free, whereas you need Amazon Prime or a $19.99-a-month Alexa Plus sub to get the Frame’s intelligent photo curation features, voice search, and photo pairing. (It includes 90 days of Alexa Plus.) Without the sub, you can just upload images to the Frame from Amazon Photos.

Compared to the competition, Alexa adds real value

At $200, the Frame is a bit too expensive. While comparable in price to the Aura and Skylight frames, it costs the same as the Echo Show 8, which has the same Alexa-powered photo curation and voice features, but adds a camera, a better, if smaller, screen (8.7 inches / 1340 x 800), better speakers, and a more functional touchscreen. You can also pay $2.99 a month to remove ads from the Show with Amazon’s Photo Gallery Unlimited subscription.

While many people don’t want or need that extra hardware of the Echo Show, it somehow feels wrong that Amazon charges the same amount for less. However, the Frame is already seeing its first big discount: It’s down to $115 for Black Friday. At that price, it’s an easy buy for households that want a smart digital photo frame that can also set a timer. If Amazon added the option of a clock, it would be almost perfect.

#158. Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

This resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled plans to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” said Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole said.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, said he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

#155. WhatsApp now lets you schedule messages in group and individual chats

WhatsApp on Wednesday started rolling out a much-sought-after feature: the ability to schedule messages in both individual and group chats.

The feature is rolling out globally to all users across iOS and Android. Once it becomes available, you can type a message and long-press the send button to schedule it. You can choose to send a message anywhere between 10 minutes and 14 days later.

Users will be able to see all their scheduled messages and delete them if needed. It’s not clear if there is a way to edit the schedule of a message.

Notably, scheduled messages will be sent even if your phone is off or outside network coverage. You can schedule messages containing text, photos, and videos.

The feature could prove useful for wishing someone a happy birthday on time or chatting with people across time zones. Businesses may also find it easier to schedule texts and updates to their customers, and people who use the app to coordinate work will likely find themselves using scheduled texts to update their teams.

WhatsApp rivals like Telegram and Signal have had the ability to schedule messages for a while now, so the Meta-owned chat app is late in rolling it out.

What can you get for $30 these days? When it comes to tech, you might be surprised. Even as gadgets get more expensive, $30 can still go a long way, especially on Black Friday. For just $8, for instance, TP-Link’s Tapo smart plug lets you control your Christmas tree lights from your phone. You can also grab a decent pair of ANC-equipped earbuds for under $20, or spend about the same on a clever set of rechargeable AAs. And it’s not just gadgets that are on sale this weekend: you can even sign up for a year of Disney Plus and Hulu for $4.99 a month.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best Black Friday deals you can still pick up for $30 or less, from charging accessories and smart home tech to earbuds, streaming subs, games, and more. Whether you’re looking for practical stocking stuffers or want to treat yourself, these are the deals that won’t put a (huge) dent in your wallet.

Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.

Who needs magnets when you have suction cups? Octobuddy’s cheap silicone mount works with most phones to provide hands-free flexibility whenever necessary. It features 24 single-sided cups, which allow you to stick your phone to a mirror, window, or any other surface you think will provide that perfect TikTok angle.

The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage. Read our hands-on.

An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.

The Clip 5 is a compact Bluetooth speaker that provides big sound. It has a customizable equalizer, so you can adjust the sound to your taste, along with an IP67 rating and up to 12 hours of playtime. It also has a built-in carabiner (hence the name), making it easy to clip the speaker to a backpack for easy listening on the go.

Hoto’s rechargeable screwdriver is ideal for small repairs. It offers three torque modes, a rotational speed of up to 220RPM, and a helpful circular LED to illuminate dark spaces. The durable case also holds all 25 steel bits and an extension bar for getting into hard-to-reach places.

Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.

Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and DreamWorks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.

The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.

Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.

The original LifeStraw was designed for those heading into the backcountry. The new LifeStraw Sip? Not so much. The reusable steel straw is geared more toward travelers than outdoor enthusiasts, though fortunately it still manages to remove about 99.99 percent of microplastics, bacteria, and parasites from your drinking water.

Anker’s 621 Magnetic Battery is a slim 5,000mAh charger that can attach magnetically to the back of any MagSafe-ready iPhone.

TP-Link’s Wi-Fi smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms to set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.

Paramount Plus Premium provides access to live sports as well as movies and shows from both platforms, including Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a host of Yellowstone spinoffs, Star Trek shows, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, Twin Peaks, Dexter, and more.

In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.

Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.

With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.

Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.

Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.

Halo: Campaign Evolved lets you revisit the original Halo: Combat Evolved campaign with better graphics, updated controls, and improved sound. The well-crafted remake also adds three new missions starring Master Chief and Sgt. Johnson that take place before the main campaign. Read our review.

No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.

The Witcher 3 lets you explore the war-torn Northern Kingdoms as Geralt of Rivia while preparing to face the mysterious Wild Hunt. The recent remaster adds improved visuals, smoother combat, and better movement, cementing the game’s status as one of the best RPGs of all time.

Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.

LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they work with any major smart home platform. The company is currently trialing a Thread beta that will bring the option to add Thread connectivity to all its Matter devices.

The ChomChom is a reusable roller that works great for removing unwanted pet hair from furniture, allowing you to skip lint rollers, vacuuming, and other cleaning tools in a pinch.

Apple TV offers ad-free streaming of original shows and movies, including shows like Severance, Silo, Slow Horses, and Pluribus. The service also features a rotating selection of films, along with live Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.

Anker’s Qi2 charging pads support wireless charging speeds of up to 15W, and their 5-foot cable shouldn’t feel constricting if you need to move the charger around.

Blink’s Mini 2K Plus is a small plug-in security camera that lets you monitor your home or pets with 2K video, motion detection, and color night vision. It also offers two-way audio, a built-in siren, and Alexa support; however, some features, including person and vehicle detection, require a Blink subscription.

Attending a live concert? You can protect your hearing with Loop’s Quiet 2 earplugs. They pack up to 24dB (SNR) of noise reduction and come with four ear tip sizes, allowing them to accommodate a range of ear shapes.

Crunchyroll is an anime-centric streaming service that offers ad-free access to shows like One Piece, Jujutsu Kaisen, The Apothecary Diaries, and Black Clover, with new episodes available shortly after they air in Japan.

Logitech’s Pop is a cute, simple wireless mouse with an ambidextrous design and the ability to switch between up to three devices. It supports customization through the Logi Options Plus app and can last for several months on a single charge.

Logitech’s G502 Hero has most of the same features as one of our top choices among gaming mice, the G502 Lightspeed, except it’s wired. If you’re okay with that, this is an excellent mouse that you can usually find for $50 or less.

The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). It also supports 480Mbps data transfer speeds and, unlike similar power meter-equipped cables, lets you turn off the screen when needed.

The Tile Pro is the company’s loudest Bluetooth tracker, one that benefits from a 500-foot range. It also features a user-replaceable battery, unlike some other Tiles, and works with both iOS and Android devices.

Anker’s jack-of-all-trades travel adapter packs enough ports to refill your devices during some downtime. It features one AC outlet, two USB-C ports (one tops out at 20W), and two USB-A ports. It’s not the fastest wall charger, but it’s a solid choice when you can find it at a discount.

The Kobo Remote lets you turn pages on a compatible Kobo e-reader with the click of a button, so you can keep reading without reaching for the screen. It connects directly over Bluetooth and features a curved, handheld design that doesn’t require clipping anything onto your e-reader.

The second-gen Ring Indoor Cam lets you keep an eye on your place in 1080p, with support for motion detection alerts, a live feed, and color night vision.

Workpro’s EDC is a lightweight folding utility knife with a side-mounted button that lets you flick it open and closed with one hand. It uses standard utility blades, which you can easily replace using a spring-loaded plate, making it handy for breaking down cardboard boxes and other tasks.

Lamicall’s cord organizers use magnetic clasps to keep cables in place, preventing them from slipping behind desks, shelves, and other furniture when unplugged.

Nalgene’s lightweight, 16-ounce water bottle features a narrow opening for sipping, a leakproof lid, and a slim design that fits in cup holders. It’s made from durable, BPA- and BPS-free plastic, with measurement markings along the side and dishwasher-safe construction.

This tiny cordless driver comes with five double-ended bits for most basic around-the-house projects and Ikea-level builds.

Amazon’s aptly titled Smart Plug doesn’t require a hub and lets you add Alexa functionality to any outlet, which, in turn, allows you to control a range of devices with just your voice.

Soundcore’s Select 4 Go is a compact Bluetooth speaker with up to 20 hours of battery life and support for stereo pairing with a second Select 4 Go. It also carries an IP67 rating for dust and water resistance, rendering it a great option for hiking or a trip to the beach.

FromSoftware’s 2022 epic, Elden Ring, takes the Dark Souls formula to a vast open world. Read our review.

#152. X’s latest update for creators focuses on vertical video

X announced new creation tools Wednesday, many of them focused on short-form vertical video. The updates are part of the platform’s effort to compete with social networks such as YouTube and Instagram as the format continues to grow in popularity.

The tools are designed to help creators make professional-quality vertical videos, share original content more easily, and earn more. They also give creators more ways to record, edit, and publish content directly on the platform without relying on third-party apps.

A key addition is an upgraded media editor that lets creators produce polished vertical videos without leaving X. Recording features include the ability to capture video in segments and use green-screen effects, the company said.

The editor also offers a range of postproduction tools. Creators can convert horizontal videos to vertical format, automatically generate captions, trim footage, add text overlays, choose custom thumbnails, and adjust photos before publishing.

Thanks to a recently announced update, users can now add up to 20 photos and videos to a single post, which audiences can swipe through horizontally. X says the feature is intended for sharing event recaps, behind-the-scenes moments, and product launches.

Availability of the new features varies by region, X said.

Earlier this month, the company introduced a clipping feature that lets users take snippets from longer videos, add their own commentary, and post the clips without leaving X. Clips credit and link to the original video, plus the person who creates a clip and the original poster can earn from its views.

Another feature, “React with Video,” launched earlier this year. Similar to TikTok’s “stitch” feature, this lets creators respond to posts with video commentary while displaying the original post in the background.

X has also introduced new earning opportunities and updates to its creator monetization programs in recent months. These include the “Video Kickstart Bonus,” an invitation-only pilot that rewards selected creators for publishing original vertical videos under three minutes long and without watermarks.

We wouldn’t normally recommend a bad camera, but we’ll make an exception for the Kodak Charmera. As my colleague Andrew Liszewski pointed out in his review, the tiny retro keychain camera takes pretty lackluster photos, yet it’s charming enough that he kept using it anyway. That makes it a great gift for anyone who loves cute gadgets, especially now that it’s on sale at Amazon and B&H Photo for an all-time low of $29.74 (about $5 off).

The Charmera is small enough to carry on your keys and comes in a blind box, so you won’t know which of the six retro designs or the rarer transparent version you’re getting until you open it. It’s a simple point-and-shoot with a tiny LCD screen, and its 1,440x1,080-pixel photos often look fuzzy and washed out. Some of the built-in effects can make the results more interesting, though. Liszewski had some fun with the black-and-white mode and found that the red, blue, yellow, and gray pixel filters could produce bolder two-tone images. Video and audio quality are poor, too, and you can’t adjust much to improve them. Still, for a $30 keychain, it offers a surprising amount to play with.

The Charmera isn’t something you’d want to rely on for an important occasion, but it can be fun to experiment with. Liszewski found that even though most pictures weren’t worth keeping, he’d occasionally get one interesting enough to share. That makes it a fun stocking stuffer for someone who loves cute, unusual gadgets.

#150. Taiwan election: DPP gains ground but loses Taipei race

Taiwan's ruling DPP has made gains in local elections, winning nine of 22 local governments. But it failed to win Taipei, where incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an defeated challenger Puma Shen.

Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) made gains in local elections on Saturday, winning nine of the island's 22 local governments, up from five in 2022.

The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) secured 12 local governments, two fewer than in the previous elections, while the Taiwan People's Party (TPP) won one city, according to local media reports.

The elections, in which voters chose mayors and county chiefs for four-year terms, are being seen as an indication of the political mood ahead of the island's 2028 presidential elections.

President Lai Ching-te campaigned for DPP candidates, while the KMT, which traditionally performs better in local polls and favours closer ties with China, sought to retain its local strongholds.

In the most closely watched contest, incumbent Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT defeated DPP challenger Puma Shen, ending the ruling party's hopes of regaining control of the capital for the first time since 1998.

Shen conceded defeat in front of thousands of supporters, saying the voters' decision must be respected.

"Whoever wins, it is a victory for Taiwan's democracy," he told supporters.

Chiang thanked voters for backing his administration, saying they had recognised the city's work over the past four years.

China is paying close attention to the local polls, despite not currently featuring as a key campaign issue. Taiwan's government had warned its people to be vigilant against fake news on social media, citing a Chinese disinformation campaign.

Taiwan's 22 cities and counties are currently focused on issues such as transport, childcare and the environment. While these issues do not directly impact the China policy, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in.

China has denounced DPP candidate Puma Shen, who was sanctioned by Beijing and is wanted by Chinese police over alleged separatist activities.

He entered the mayoral race as an underdog but had managed to ride a political wave that drew huge crowds to his campaign rallies.

Nevertheless, the DPP announced Saturday evening that Shen had lost his bid for mayor, which was seen as a longshot as Taipei has not elected a DPP mayor in nearly 30 years.

Earlier this month, Shen said Chinese police had never contacted him and that whoever wins, Taipei's election would be a victory for democracy in the face of pressure from Beijing.

Taipei turning to a progressive candidate in what has traditionally been a KMT stronghold would be seen as "quite shameful" in Beijing, Austin Wang, political science professor at the University of Nevada, told AFP news agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China claims Taiwan as part of its territory under its "One China" principle and has recently increased pressure on Taiwan to accept its sovereignty claims, threatening force to seize the island.

Mayor Chiang campaigned against Shen, also pulling in thousands of supporters to his rallies.  Chiang is seen as a potential future presidential candidate.

Analysts have cautioned that the local elections are not a reliable barometer of how people might vote for the presidential elections in 2028. Still, Saturday's results could influence the selection process for the KMT presidential candidate.

The DPP is likely to rally behind President Lai for a reelection.

The most likely KMT candidates are Taichung's outgoing Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han  Kuo-yu.

KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who's pro-Beijing stance has even alienated her from many in the party, is also viewed as a potential challenger for the party's nomination. However, she could face pressure to step down if KMT performs poorly in the local elections.

#148. Character.AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats challenged by state AGs

What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.

Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.

The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.

Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.

In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.

“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.

“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”

Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”

The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.)

Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.

California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

#146. DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers

The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.

According to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”

But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.

Price is a major factor, unsurprisingly, but for the holidays, some people care more about novelty above all else. They just want to gift something cool (or get something nice for themselves).

Deals on streaming services were extremely popular with readers this year because the savings are outstanding, and I think most of us are sick of paying an arm and a leg for monthly access. You can save big on Disney Plus, Hulu, HBO Max, Peacock, and even Apple TV. Streaming aside, Verge readers proved they have good taste in gear, as you can see below in our small collection of the most-bought products.

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.

You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.

Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.

With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available.
