#97. Sakana AI’s CEO says its homegrown models are about more than Japan’s national security

Sakana AI, a Japanese AI startup, last month revealed plans to develop its own foundation model. The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies.

Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the company’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI. In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited.

“When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do. This is our long-term vision,” Ha said. “But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.”

Sakana will begin working on Sawara this month, aiming to train and release a smaller-scale model in early 2027, followed by a larger version.

The project comes roughly five months after Sakana launched Fugu, an AI orchestration system that ropes in other large language models, including those developed by U.S. AI labs, to assemble AI agents according to the task at hand. The Tokyo-based startup has also built Namazu, a Japanese-focused language model that fine-tunes existing open-weight models from Meta and DeepSeek to better understand Japanese language, culture, and business needs, including translation, political questions, and AI agent tasks.

“We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said. “They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics […] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.”

However, Ha acknowledged that developing a domestic foundation model alone will not fully eliminate reliance on foreign AI technology.

“The only thing [left] for us to become a full-stack company is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued. “We plan to apply the [Sawara] technology in industry and manufacturing. We’ll train both a small and a large model next year. The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions. Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.”

While Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications. For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises.

“Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha said. “People often point to Palantir and other systems. I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog. But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.”

Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, on systems for detecting disinformation.

Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha said. Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises.

“Those lessons helped us plan how to develop and deploy Sawara. I think similar requirements exist in many governments,” he said.

While enterprise customers can use a combination of Fugu, Namazu and AI models developed overseas, Sakana’s government-related work currently focuses on two main areas: disinformation detection and analysis, and multimodal systems that integrate data from different government sources.

Sakana’s expansion into developing its own foundation models comes amid speculation about a potential IPO following reports by Nikkei and Bloomberg earlier this month.

But Ha said the company doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public.

The reported timing and potential valuation were speculative, Ha said, adding that he did not know when the company might pursue a listing, though he expects his startup to eventually go public in Japan itself.

“We have a gravitational pull to eventually IPO in Japan,” Ha said.

Ha sees Sakana’s future growth tied to the global expansion of Japanese manufacturers. Rather than focusing on selling its models, the company wants to help local companies use AI to become more competitive globally.

“We want to strategically work with the government and Japanese industrial base, make them competitive,” Ha said. “We want to go abroad, go international together with manufacturing and industrial sectors.”

#96. Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter

Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% â way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

Zelensky's ratings have dipped considerably

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method â sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia â "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a cafÃ© here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Tens of thousands of soldiers have died since the outbreak of war

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (Â£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

#94. This new sports app is designed specifically for women’s sports

A new sports app is looking to change the way fans engage with women’s sports, and it’s doing so without the real-money gambling that has become increasingly common in the sports world.

Called Rival, the app officially launched last weekend on the App Store and Google Play Store, timed to coincide with the National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) Championship.

With Rival, users can make free-to-play picks, earn points, compete on leaderboards, create and join groups, and connect with other fans. The platform also serves as a hub for discovering women’s sports, bringing together schedules, scores, news, highlights, and information on where to watch.

The app is the brainchild of Kelly DiPaola, whose previous experience includes working for Barbra Streisand and producing unscripted television, including Netflix’s “Selling Sunset.” The idea grew out of her frustration with traditional sports apps, which tend to prioritize scores and statistics over the fan experience. Rather than simply creating another place to check game results, DiPaola envisioned a destination dedicated to women’s sports, where fans could build connections, find community, and feel more invested in the games they follow.

“I’m a passionate sports fan, and my partner, Jodie Taylor, is a former England Lioness and now Technical Director at Arsenal Women,” DiPaola told TechCrunch in an email. “The original spark was my frustration with the disparity in women’s sports coverage on traditional sports betting platforms. I’ve never been particularly good at accepting inequality as the status quo, so I decided to do something about it.”

That vision comes at a time when women’s sports are experiencing record growth in attendance and viewership. Yet greater visibility doesn’t necessarily translate into a better experience for fans, particularly women who participate in mainstream sports communities online.

Platforms such as Reddit, X, and sports-focused forums can expose women — especially women of color and LGBTQ+ athletes — to harassment, abuse, and discriminatory commentary.

The problem is well documented. A 2024 NCAA study found that online abuse targeting student-athletes peaked during March Madness, with women’s basketball players receiving three times as many threats as their male counterparts.

Rival is positioning itself as an alternative to that experience, placing positive social connection and community at the center of its platform. Users can create profiles and statuses, follow other users, and create or join groups around their favorite teams and sports.

“Women’s sports doesn’t just have a visibility problem. It has a participation problem,” DiPaola said. “I wanted to build somewhere that felt like walking into your favorite local bar on a Friday night, where you could turn up on your own and still feel like you belonged, like you were part of something bigger than yourself.”

Although the app is focused on women’s teams and competitions, anyone can join. The platform also includes blocking and reporting tools, private profiles, private groups, in-app support, and moderation features designed to address abusive behavior.

“Our responsibility is to create a safe and welcoming environment for everyone,” DiPaola said. “We have zero tolerance for abuse, harassment, or discrimination, and accounts engaging in such behavior are subject to removal. As our community grows, our moderation capabilities will need to grow with it.”

Another major differentiator is Rival’s decision to avoid real-money sports betting altogether. Instead, the platform centers on what the company describes as “friendly competition,” allowing users to make predictions and compete with friends without putting money on the line.

That distinction is particularly timely as sports betting continues to expand across the U.S., raising concerns about its consequences. According to the American Gaming Association, Americans wagered $166.94 billion on legal sports betting last year. A UCLA study found that, in states allowing online sports gambling, the likelihood of a personal bankruptcy filing increased by around 25%.

At launch, Rival covers 36 leagues and competitions, 1,979 teams, and more than 20,000 athletes internationally. This includes NCAA Women’s Basketball, NCAA Softball, Women’s Professional Football League, EuroLeague, and more.

DiPaola says the company ultimately wants to represent every sport women play, including those that have historically received less coverage. That will mean exploring partnerships to improve data availability for underrepresented sports and leagues.

Looking ahead, Rival also plans to expand its sports coverage, develop its live-picks ecosystem, introduce “richer” social and community features, and bring fan participation closer to live broadcasts.

#93. Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

China thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

#92. Ukraine's expertise comes in handy for international drone alliances

Ukrainian expertise merged with Europe's financial and industrial clout: Germany and other countries are expanding drone partnerships with Ukraine and reshaping Europe's defense industry in the process.

Germany and Ukraine want to further boost their defense cooperation. Following a meeting in Berlin with his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced that drones for Ukraine will be manufactured in Germany in the future.

The project involves the Ukrainian reconnaissance drone known as the "Babka" ("Dragonfly"). Germany is investing around €34 million in the project, according to Pistorius. German company Wingcopter and Ukrainian manufacturer Shadow Flytech have established a joint venture specifically for this purpose.

This is far from the first cooperation agreement of its kind that Kyiv has launched with its European partners. The initiatives include numerous joint ventures between Ukrainian companies and defense contractors across Europe.

In July 2026, the EU and Ukraine launched a joint "Drone Alliance." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reached an agreement to establish the initiative. The alliance focuses on joint development, industrial production, supply chains and counter-drone defense. One of its key goals is to combine Ukrainian technologies proven in combat with Europe's industrial production capabilities. The agreement on the Babka drones is also part of this alliance.

As part of its Drone Deal strategy, Ukraine has sealed long-term bilateral agreements with several countries. These include the Netherlands, Norway, Finland and the Baltic states, as well as Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Kyiv is also in negotiations with around a dozen other countries.

The cooperation covers four main areas: joint drone production; the exchange of intelligence and battlefield experience; cooperation in intelligence gathering, electronic warfare and cyber defense; and the training and advising of military personnel.

Although Germany has not yet formally joined the long-term Drone Deal framework, negotiations are afoot. German companies are already deeply involved in Ukraine's drone industry via several cooperation agreements.

This week, Ukraine and the United Kingdom also agreed on a new deal under which the UK will manufacture Ukrainian medium and long-range drones. In March, the two countries agreed to produce Ukraine's "Octopus" interceptor drone under license in the UK.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the start of the war against Russia in the Donbas in 2014, Ukraine has developed a small but highly innovative drone industry. Up until 2022, however, the country only made a limited number of military drones.

With the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, development and production expanded dramatically. Before the full-scale war, only seven drone models had received state approval. By 2023, that number had risen to 67. By early 2024, around 200 companies were operating in Ukraine's drone sector.

"Perhaps some people underestimated the fact that Ukraine is not just an industrial country, but also a country of engineers, with a strong science and technology education system and a well-developed software industry," German security expert Nico Lange, director of the Berlin-based Institute for Risk Analysis and International Security (IRIS), told DW.

Ukraine has since massively expanded its domestic production capacity. According to Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, as of June 2026, 95% of the drones procured for its armed forces are now manufactured domestically.

The key question is whether Ukraine has sufficient funding, components and secure production facilities to meet demand over the long term.

Drones are used at many levels of military operations. They come in various forms, including attack, interceptor and reconnaissance drones, and operate both in the air and at sea. They are significantly less expensive than many other weapons systems and, because of their small size and the sheer numbers in which they are deployed, can be difficult to defend against.

However, drones are mass-produced, and many of them, particularly small attack drones, are often destroyed after just a single mission or neutralized by electronic jamming.

In July 2026, Zelenskyy said Ukraine could manufacture around 10 million drones domestically each year. The goal, however, was to increase production to 20 million annually with support from European partners.

For a long time, supply chains remained a major challenge for Ukraine. As recently as early 2024, around 90% of all drone components — including motors, control chips and cameras — came from China.

"Traditionally, Chinese components have played an important role in the drone industry because of their lower cost," Nico Lange explains. "There are efforts to manufacture these components domestically, but that cannot happen overnight."

Through its defense cooperation agreements, Kyiv has managed to reduce the share of components imported directly from China to around 28% in the first eight months of 2026.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Ukraine, access to Western supply chains for urgently needed components is a major benefit of the defense cooperation with Europe. Another advantage is that relocating production facilities abroad helps protect them from Russian attacks. Many of the agreements also provide for Ukraine to contribute the technology and battlefield experience, while its European partner supplies most of the funding and industrial capacity.

In the long run, however, Ukraine's most important reason for pursuing these partnerships is likely its ambition to establish itself as a lasting member of Europe's defense community and integrate its military into the European security architecture.

"What began as donations of weapons, ammunition and other equipment in the early stages of the war has evolved into a strategic partnership that offers significant benefits to both sides," says defense expert Lange. "It has rightly been described as a partnership between equals."

This article was originally written in German.

#89. OpenAI’s new countersuit accuses Apple of ‘unlawfully pressuring vendors’

After Apple sued OpenAI this summer over allegations that the AI company had stolen trade secrets, OpenAI has fired back with a countersuit of its own.

According to Bloomberg, the new suit claims that as OpenAI prepared to enter the hardware market, Apple responded by “by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI and using expansive employment restraints to limit OpenAI’s access to talented engineers.”

The suit also accuses Apple of stealing OpenAI’s trade secrets.

Apple told the Financial Times that the countersuit is “a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple’s confidential information.”

Apple previously alleged that OpenAI leaders, including Chief Hardware Officer Tang Tan, asked candidates to bring Apple hardware components to their job interviews and coached them on how to evade security procedures. OpenAI responded that it has “no interest in other companies’ trade secrets.”

The dueling lawsuits mark a dramatic souring of the relationship between two companies that in 2024 partnered to integrate OpenAI’s ChatGPT with Apple’s Siri.

#87. Watch: BBC confronts German man suspected of supplying migrant gangs with small boats

A German boat dealer is suspected of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings to the UK, in the first four months of 2026, allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

#80. Azerbaijan's opposition leader Ali Karimli: A year behind bars

Azerbaijani opposition leader Ali Karimli has been in prison since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of attempting to seize power by force, but human rights groups say his prosecution is politically motivated.

A year after his arrest, Azerbaijani opposition leader Ali Karimli remains in prison.

Karimli has denied charges of attempting to seize power by force, calling them politically motivated. He is the chairman of the Azerbaijani Popular Front Party (APFP), one of the country's main opposition parties.

Karimli is on trial alongside Mammad Ibrahim, his longtime political adviser and a senior party official. Ibrahim has previously served time in prison. In 2016, he was sentenced to three years on hooliganism charges that Human Rights Watch described as spurious. He was detained on November 29, 2025, alongside Karimli.

Azerbaijan's State Security Service has charged Karimli and Ibrahim under Article 278.1 of the Criminal Code, which covers actions aimed at forcibly seizing power or changing the country's constitutional order. A conviction could carry a prison sentence of 12 to 20 years, or life imprisonment.

In a statement issued on February 12, the State Security Service alleged that Karimli had conspired with the former head of Azerbaijan's Presidential Administration, Ramiz Mehdiyev, and his allies to seize state power. The agency also linked the alleged conspiracy to interference by foreign intelligence services in Azerbaijan's political affairs.

According to investigators, Karimli planned to exploit a mass rally in Baku in July 2020, originally held in support of the Azerbaijani army, to provoke unrest and seize the parliament and state television buildings. In a 15-page copy of a court motion obtained by DW from the APFP leadership, Karimli said he did not attend the rally and that his party was not involved in organizing it.

Nazim Musayev, a lawyer representing Mammad Ibrahim, told DW that both defendants considered the prosecution politically motivated. Shortly after the arrest, Amnesty International demanded that Azerbaijani authorities release Karimli "unless they can demonstrate reasonable evidence of an alleged criminal offence."

"Karimli's detention is the latest outrage in the ongoing consolidation of authoritarian practices in Azerbaijan," said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty's deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, in a statement on December 1, 2025. "There appear to be no limits to the government's campaign to crush all political opposition and suppress all dissent in the country."

In the court motion obtained by DW, submitted at a preliminary hearing on November 3, Karimli made no secret of his desire for political change in Azerbaijan. However, he insisted he has always opposed using violence to achieve it.

"I accept only one way of coming to power — through democratic elections," Karimli wrote. The court rejected his call for charges to be dropped, but added the motion to his case file.

Karimli also disputed the prosecution's claims about the National Council of Democratic Forces, an opposition coalition formed in 2013. He said the group was established openly to support a joint opposition candidate in the presidential election rather than to organize a coup.

Karimli has also denied any cooperation with Mehdiyev, the ex-head of the presidential administration, saying the two have never met or communicated and that they represented opposing political positions for decades. Mehdiyev's lawyer told DW that his client also denies any connection to Karimli.

The trial against Karimli and Ibrahim is held behind closed doors, with foreign diplomats also being denied entry. Lawyer Nazim Musayev said the closed proceedings were justified on the grounds that the case involved state secrets.

In his motion, Karimli expressed little confidence in the fairness of the proceedings, argued that the case is intended to remove him from political life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Karimli's son Turkel, who lives in the United States, told DW that he last spoke to his father in late April or early May. He said his mother had also been denied phone calls and face-to-face visits since June.

Turkel said his father's detention conditions had deteriorated sharply over the summer. Citing information received from lawyers, he said the authorities had temporarily stopped accepting food parcels from the family and restricted the amount of additional drinking water, which had been limited to 5 liters (1.3 gallons) a week. According to Amnesty International, Karimli reportedly fainted from severe dehydration during an August 6 court hearing.

Food deliveries were later permitted again, and lawyers were told earlier this month that the water allowance would be increased to 10 liters a week. Karimli's legal team said he has lost considerable weight during his time in prison.

Karimli has also complained of persistent noise disrupting his sleep, restrictions on family contact and physical exercise, worsening back pain and poor ventilation in his cell.

Rights groups have raised concerns about Karimli's detention conditions, with Amnesty International warning that the reported lack of access to clean drinking water and ventilation could amount to torture or other ill treatment.

Ibrahim's family is concerned that he is not receiving adequate medical treatment in the detention facility. His son Turan Ibrahim, who lives abroad, told DW that his father suffers from kidney problems and insomnia.

According to Turan, doctors appointed by the authorities have examined his father several times. The family has also consulted outside doctors and is trying to arrange medication for him.

Turan said communication and family visits were sometimes difficult for his father. Ibrahim's wife delivers food and supplies to the detention facility once a week, and is allowed to see him through a glass partition twice a month.

Turan said his mother, who is unemployed and lives in rented accommodation, has also faced financial difficulties since her husband's arrest.

Karimli has led the APFP since 2000. The party has continued operating during his detention.

Rahim Hajiyev, a founding member of the party who now lives in France, told DW that the APFP had long relied on collective decision-making and that Karimli's arrest had not brought its organizational activities to a halt.

However, he said party members, particularly those active on social media, continued to face short-term administrative detention. Hajiyev described Karimli's arrest as part of a broader campaign against political opposition.

Karimli's detention has also drawn criticism from international organizations and European lawmakers.

On October 8, the European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for the immediate and unconditional release of Karimli and other political prisoners in Azerbaijan. Lawmakers also urged the authorities to ensure adequate medical care, access to lawyers and contact with family members. Earlier this month, Karimli was awarded the 2026 Magnitsky Human Rights Award.

Karimli's case was also raised at a joint press conference in Baku on November 18, attended by Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and his German counterpart, Johann Wadephul. Asked about Karimli's arrest, Bayramov said that belonging to the opposition did not exempt anyone from legal responsibility.

Bayramov maintained that the case was being handled in accordance with Azerbaijani law and said the court would make the final decision.

#79. Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

#75. Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study

Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.

More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.

The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.

Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.

India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed

South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.

The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.

Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.

More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage

Marital rape: Delhi high court gives split verdict

India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.

Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.

Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries

"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.

"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."

The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.

In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.

Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.

There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.

But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it

India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.

"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.

"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."

Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.

Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.

In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

#72. Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves

A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.

"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.

The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".

Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.

Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.

The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.

Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:

assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child

facilitating the commission of a terrorist act

being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.

Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.

A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.

"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.

Stephen Mwiti, who lost six children to the cult, welcomed the conviction of Mackenzie for murder last month

When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.

The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

#71. AI-generated lawsuits flood German courts

German courts are being overwhelmed by AI-generated lawsuits, many riddled with errors and running to huge lengths. Some state justice ministers want to introduce a fee to stem the flow, but that brings its own problems.

German courts are reporting a huge rise in lawsuits and complaints, and are blaming the use of artificial intelligence models.

The German media has been filled with reports about the problem, which particularly affects social courts, where citizens can file complaints themselves without legal representation. In most such cases, people appeal against sanctions or cuts to their unemployment benefits, or demands from authorities that benefits be returned, but the complaints can also pertain to other benefits or sudden rises in health insurance contributions.

Marcus Howe, spokesperson for Berlin's state social court, where he is himself a judge, said his court was dealing with 28% more cases this year than in 2025.

"That is of course an enormous increase, which is surely in part because of artificial intelligence," he told DW, though he added that it could also be partly down to the tightening of sanctions on unemployment benefits, introduced by the federal government this year.

Other states have reported similar increases. The Legal Tribune Online news portal reported that the number of urgent proceedings at the eight social courts in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state, rose from around 1,400 in the first quarter of 2025 to 3,600 in the same period of 2026.

Howe said that in most cases it's still easy for judges to see when a complaint has been generated by AI.

"You can usually tell at first glance," he said. "The font and the layout are different. In the worst cases, they're much too long and bloated, stuffed with content that has very little to do with the case."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Howe has also noticed that the AI-generated lawsuits are more impersonal, which makes his job more difficult.

"You don't really get an impression of what kind of people are behind these cases," he said. "And it becomes difficult to recognize what the actual problem is. The human factor is important because a lot of this computer-generated German can mislead you. It makes arguments that the computer has thought up, but which aren't actually important for the people in question."

This can go to extremes: Friedrich-Johannes Graf von Pfeil, president of the social court in Potsdam, Brandenburg, has received one complaint that stretched to 800 pages.

"You can tell very quickly when one is AI-generated, just because they use specialist legal formulations that no ordinary citizen would use," he told DW. "There's often very little on the facts of the case, and a lot of legal interpretation that no non-specialist could provide. But you still have to respond to all of it."

The problem for judges is that they are obliged to wade through all this material, which often includes references to other legal rulings that either have little bearing on the case — or have been hallucinated by the AI tool.

Nor can the courts simply use their own AI tools to summarize these documents, von Pfeil said. "If we wanted to use AI to assess a legal document, we'd have security and data protection problems, because the AI isn't in-house," he said. "Also, we receive a lot of sensitive medical documents that would end up on a server that doesn't belong to the judiciary. And that's not allowed."

At a regular conference this month, Germany's state and federal justice ministers agreed to set up a working group to look into the problem, with some conservative ministers calling for a fee to file urgent complaints.

Christian Heinz, Christian Democrat justice minister in the state of Hesse, said that a fee of €15 ($16.40) should be considered. Another proposal was for people to pay court costs for lawsuits that are deemed to have little chance of success or which abuse the system.

The VdK, a social welfare association that offers legal advice to people dealing with German welfare authorities, is vehemently against those ideas. Holger Lange, head of the VdK's federal legal department, thinks it's vital that people — particularly the most vulnerable — have access to social courts without fearing the costs.

The solution, as far as Lange is concerned, is not to "build walls around the courts," but to streamline their digital access and make it easier to submit clear, concise complaints — in other words, online portals with easy-to-understand questions and word limits on legal documents. "They could steer the procedure a little," he told DW.

Howe is also skeptical of fees, an idea that, he said, has been discussed for decades. But social courts are supposed to have low thresholds to entry, he added: "This isn't a situation that suddenly justifies fees — yet. We want to keep access to justice open."

Judge von Pfeil thinks a fee would be "worth a try," though he acknowledges that a lot of people might apply for legal aid, which means the state would end up with more bureaucracy and costs anyway.

Though there has been a recent increase in social court complaints, a broader look at the statistics shows that this is nothing that the social courts haven't seen before.

In the years leading up to the advent of wide availability of AI chatbots, the courts actually saw a big drop in the number of pending cases: from over 445,000 at the end of 2017 to 325,000 at the end of 2024. Analysts suggest that such long-term developments are tied to economic conditions and legal changes in unemployment benefits.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And Lange doesn't think that this new rise in complaints — AI-generated or not — is necessarily a bad sign. "The key thing is enabling people," he said. "We need to ask whether the recent rise isn't also in part the expression of a demand for legal protection that has been hidden so far, because people just haven't dared to claim their rights."

Lange acknowledged that AI-generated complaints can't always be trusted, because of errors and hallucinations. But he stressed that the use of AI doesn't make an appeal invalid.

"It could be a seriously ill person whose pension claim has just been refused," he said. "Or a care-dependent person who desperately needs support. We always need to look at who is behind the complaint."

#70. Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants

Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".

Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill

Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.

Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.

"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.

The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.

"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."

Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laÃ¯citÃ© - as a core component of its identity.

Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.

The leader of the Bloc QuÃ©bÃ©cois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.

"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-FranÃ§ois Blanchet told reporters in French.

#68. 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged

How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade

Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.

"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.

Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (Â£267,000) in just a few hours.

Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.

On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.

The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather

Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving

Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.

"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.

"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"

The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.

There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.

Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.

"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.

He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".

"We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."

Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.

ââThis canât be happeningâ,â Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the bandâs reactions.

"They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."

The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - said it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars

Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the NÄ Koa AliÊ»i HawaiÊ»i All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.

Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.

The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.

"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.

But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".

The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.

New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade

Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.

"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."

Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.

"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.

By Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," said Houser.

While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.

Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.

#63. Two American Airlines planes clip wings before takeoff at Reagan airport

A piece of aircraft is seen on the ground after two jets clipped wings at Reagan National Airport

Two American Airlines jets hit each other at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while taxiing for departure in Washington DC on Friday.

One jet "clipped the wing" of the other at around 5:10 ET (22:10 GMT), the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate.

Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service to be inspected by maintenance teams, American Airlines said.

The incident happened at the same airport where 67 people died in a deadly collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025.

"American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said.

Air traffic controllers can be heard on an audio recording saying two Boeing 737s clipped on the airport's runway. The controllers requested an emergency response and fire personnel to the plane, then directed the aircraft to return to the gate.

The "wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact", American Airlines said in a statement. The airline added that it is working to get affected passengers who were evacuated from both planes to their destinations as soon as possible.

A passenger on flight 2152 headed to Chicago's O'Hare airport told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as they were taxiing before departure. The other plane, flight 638, was bound for Dallas-Fort Worth airport.

The passenger added that the "aircraft shook quite violently" upon impact and he heard gasps inside the cabin. He described the moment as "tense", but that nobody seemed to be hurt.

As the passenger looked out the window he saw what appeared to be the tip of the aircraft wing

As he looked out the window, he saw a piece of the aircraft on the ground. It looked like the "tip of the wing", he said, describing how the other aircraft's wing was overlapping his plane's wing.

The BBC has contacted American Airlines about reports of the broken wingtip.

As they taxied back to the gate, the passenger said he saw a truck pick up the piece that had fallen.

The fact that this isn't the first incident at this airport was "definitely scary", the passenger said.

Last year, there was a deadly mid-air collision between another American Airlines flight and a military helicopter at Reagan National.

The 64 people on the passenger plane and three US Army members on the Black Hawk helicopter all died in the crash.

The aircraft, en route to land at the DC airport after leaving from Wichita, Kansas, was sent careening into the Potomac River upon impact with the military helicopter.

It was later determined that the helicopter was receiving faulty altitude data, causing it to fly higher than intended.

Reagan National Airport is the smaller of the two DC-area airports and caters mostly to domestic flights.

It sits right near the sprawl of the US capital, the White House and the Pentagon.

Earlier this week, the US Army said it planned to resume helicopter test flights near Reagan airport, according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner. The flights were paused following last year's incident.

BBC has contacted the Pentagon for comment.
