#61. Germany news: Leftist BSW rules out limiting ties with far-right AfD

A motion had been filed by senior BSW leaders to reject any "de facto" support of a far-right government. Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht has said limited cooperation could provide a "window of opportunity." More on DW.

Follow along for the top headlines and analysis from Germany on the Saturday, November 28 and Sunday, November 29:

The Christmas market on Munich’s Prater Island is anything but typical. Instead of the usual holiday fare, it's all about Harry Potter.

Until December 6, visitors can purchase fan merchandise, enjoy food and drinks inspired by the Harry Potter universe, and have their picture taken against a Harry Potter–inspired backdrop.

According to the organizers, the market was inspired by the HBO series Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, which premieres on December 25. The series is based on the world-famous fantasy novel series by author J.K. Rowling.

The left-wing populist party Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (also BSW) voted against a measure that would have limited cooperation with the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) on the federal level.

During the party conference in the eastern city of Dresden, a majority of the approximately 600 delegates voted against a motion put forth by several founding BSW members calling for a clearer distinction from the far right.

The basis for the vote came after the AfD came out on top in September's state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt with 39 seats. The victory is being seen as a major win for Germany's far right. In October, the AfD's Tobias Rausch in Saxony-Anhalt became Germany's first far-right state parliament speaker since World War II.

With the BSW's five seats, the two parties on the opposite extremes of the political spectrum would combine for a majority of the 83 seats.

BSW Party founder Sahra Wagenknecht and party leader Fabio De Masi have advocated for the-called "Magdeburg Model," named after the capital of Saxony-Anhalt.

This approach rejects a formal coalition with the AfD, offers no support for AfD candidate in the election of a state premiere, and calls for no official tolerance for far-fight platforms. However, the approach envisions joint motions, joint voting, and possibly also written agreements with the AfD.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Saturday, Wagenknecht made clear she does not see the AfD as a long-term strategic partner.

"None of us wants to cozy up to the AfD," Wagenknecht said. But the BSW will decide how to proceed if there is "the possibility of reasonable majorities for peace, social improvement, and a reform of public broadcasting."

The AfD and BSW see some overlap in Germany's approach to the Ukraine war, with both taking pro-Russia views critical of military support for Kyiv, while opposing or questioning sanctions on Russia, arguing that they harm the German economy.

BSW executive board members such as Christian Leye, Amid Rabieh and Klaus Ernst had sought to pass the amendment to both rule out coalitions with the AfD, and also "any formal or de facto tolerance, support for an AfD-led government, and long-term agreements on cooperation."

"Since when have we been partners with the AfD?" Leye said after the vote. "This party can only be an opponent."

"In my view, it is a racist party, a nationalist party that also has its issues with democracy. That is why it cannot be a partner," he said.

Germany's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, has classified the AfD as right-wing extremist.

Sahra Wagenknecht, the leader of the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (also BSW), has spoken at her party's conference.

She defended the party's decision to work with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), saying they needed to take advantage of the opportunity.

"The AfD is a contradictory party," she said, adding: "But as long as there is a window of opportunity for concrete changes and improvements, we must make use of it."

The BSW's ambiguous relationship with the AfD has sparked debate within the party. The BSW has left-wing economic policies but takes a hard approach to migration.

At the conference on Saturday, BSW co-founder Klaus Ernst threatened to leave the party if it didn't draw a clear line between itself and the far right.

Wagenknecht said it was not necessary for party members to "lecture each other about what unsavory characters can sometimes be found in the AfD and just how far this party is from us in terms of its platform."

Germany has paid around €16.5 million ($18 million) to victims of terrorist and extremist attacks since the 2016 attack on the Berlin Christmas market, Federal Victim Commissioner Roland Weber has said.

"The number of people affected by these attacks is almost 3,000," Weber said.

Following the Berlin attacks alone, almost €4 million was paid out in hardship funds, according to the commissioner.

The Berlin attack was a turning point in such hardship funds, according to Weber, who said structures have been built up to respond to such situations since then.

The attack took place on December 19, 2016, when Tunisian man Anis Amri drove a truck into the middle of a busy Christmas market in the capital. Some 13 people were killed and another 109 were injured. Another 43 people, bereaved relatives, also received support.

Weber said that letters were quickly sent out to those impacted by a similar attack on a Christmas market in Magdeburg on December 20, 2024, letting them know that support was available.

The German Motor Trade Association (ZDK) predicts that more than 1 million electric vehicles will be sold in Germany in 2027.

The prediction was based on its estimate of 840,000 sales in 2026.

From January to October 2026, the Federal Motor Transport Authority recorded around 698,000 new all-electric cars.

The forecast also included a total of around 3.05 million passenger cars sold, up by 2.5%.

ZDK President Thomas Peckruhn said the electric car market would gain "further momentum" in 2027. "The range of models is growing, and government subsidies for electric cars can provide additional incentives to buy."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Andrea Nahles, the head of the Federal Employment Agency (BfA), has warned that it could take months to see any noticeable recovery in the German job market.

She told the Funke media group that there would be little change between spring and early summer. Even if there's continued economic growth, its impact on the job market would be delayed.

"We've reached a tipping point," Nahles said. "For the first time, we're not seeing any growth in the number of employees subject to social insurance contributions, which currently stands at around 34 million."

She predicted that "demographics and the resulting worsening shortage of skilled workers will be the biggest problem facing the German labor market."

At the same time, there is no lack of unskilled workers. "There are currently 13 unemployed people for every open position for unskilled workers," she added.

At the same time, there are two jobs for every skilled worker.

The employment agency chief said it was necessary to attract more skilled immigrants.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

You join us the day after the German Bundestag passed the government budget for 2027, even as EU budget talks in Brussels have been faltering.

Saturday is also the party convention for the left-wing populist BSW party.

For the latest on this and more, keep reading.

#59. Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".

The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.

Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.

So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".

"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.

Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."

He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.

"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.

Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.

Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.

But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.

"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.

"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."

He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.

"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."

Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.

On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.

Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".

He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.

But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.

Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.

Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.

They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.

"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.

"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."
